## Pañcapakaraṇa Mūlaṭīkā
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One
## Dhātukathā-pakaraṇa Mūlaṭīkā
## Explanation of the Introduction to the Text
To show the time when the Blessed One taught the Dhātukathā-pakaraṇa, or to show that the text taught immediately after the Vibhaṅga is indeed the Dhātukathā-pakaraṇa, the words beginning with 'Aṭṭhārasahi' were spoken. In those words beginning with 'Aṭṭhārasahi', the Blessed One is praised as 'Mārabhañjana' (Conqueror of Māra) because He destroyed the five Māras at the foot of the Bodhi tree: Devaputta-māra, by overcoming his power and transcending his domain of the sense-sphere; Kilesa-māra and Abhisaṅkhāra-māra, by ensuring they would never arise again in His continuity; and Khandha-māra and Maccu-māra, by abandoning their cause (samudaya) and knowing them with full understanding (pariññā). This destruction was independent of others and unsurpassed. In that verse, He is called 'Mārabhañjana' because He destroyed the five Māras; or He is called 'Mārabhañjana' because He only destroys the five Māras and not other enemies such as rival kings. He is called 'Mahāvīra' (Great Hero) because He progressed courageously without fear or retreat, and because He possessed great energy (vīriya).

The states beginning with the aggregates (khandha) and ending with the 'araṇa' states are called 'elements' (dhātu) in the sense of their intrinsic nature (sabhāva), or in the sense of being the basis for the discourse of the Abhidhamma. Because this text teaches such elements, it receives the name 'Dhātukathā'. Although these natures are taught in other texts like the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, this text alone is named 'Dhātukathā' because it teaches all those natures in detail according to each of the fourteen methods, such as inclusion (saṅgaha) and exclusion (asaṅgaha). In other texts, only a partial teaching is given.

Alternatively, the methods of inclusion, exclusion, etc., of the states beginning with the aggregates and ending with the 'araṇa' states are taught by means of aggregates, bases (āyatana), and elements. In that teaching, those with a broad scope...
2: It should be understood that this text is named 'Dhātukathā' because it is a discourse (kathā) concerning elements (dhātu) by means of elements. He is called 'Dhātubhedappakāsana' (Revealer of the divisions of elements) because He clearly revealed the various divisions of elements, such as two-fold, three-fold, six-fold, and eighteen-fold. The word 'Tassatthaṃ' means the meaning (attha) of that Dhātukathā text. It should be understood that the letter 'a' in 'atthaṃ' and the letter 'ā' in 'tassā' are elided. Alternatively, in the phrase 'yaṃ dhātukathaṃ', there is an elided word 'pakaraṇaṃ'. Since this is a commentary (aṭṭhakathā) that explains the seven texts in order, when connected with that word 'pakaraṇa', the meaning of that text is expressed as 'tassatthaṃ', where the letter 'a' in 'tassa' is elided. 'Taṃ' means 'listen to the words explaining that meaning', or 'attend to and remember that meaning by listening to the words explaining it'. 'Samāhitā' means those whose minds are not distracted by various activities, or those who have well-placed the teaching in their own minds. ## The explanation of the introduction to the text is finished.

## 1. Maatikaavaṇṇanā
## 1. Nayamātikāvaṇṇanā
If it is asked, 'What is the scope of this text?', that scope is not mentioned here because it has already been stated in the Aṭṭhasālinī commentary. To show this, it is said: 'It is stated that it is divided into fourteen kinds.' The teaching of the aggregates and so on is led or proceeded by these (methods like inclusion and exclusion); or the aggregates and so on are themselves led or known by these modes; therefore, they are called 'Naya' (methods). The 'Nayamātikā' is the matrix or the summary of these methods, or the methods themselves are the matrix. These fourteen terms such as inclusion and exclusion are called 'Mūlamātikā' (Root Matrix) because they are the root foundation and the support for this text which analyzes the states such as the aggregates.

## 2. Abbhantaramātikāvaṇṇanā
By the terms such as 'pañcakkhandhā' (five aggregates), the terms such as the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha) are shown. In the teaching of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), the term 'paṭiccasamuppāda' applies to each of the twelve factors; thus, the twelve terms representing those factors are shown. By means of those terms such as the aggregates thus shown, and by means of terms such as contact (phassa) shown in their individual essence, it is said: 'by one hundred and twenty-five terms'. Among those (125 terms), kamma-bhava, upapatti-bhava, and kāma-bhava, which are analyzed in this text, are included in 'existence' (bhava) by way of their nature of causing to be or coming to be. Just as sorrow (soka) and so on are undesirable like aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), and because they are suffering rooted in that aging and death, they are included within aging and death; thus, the twelve-fold nature of dependent origination should be understood. Here, the teacher, by taking states like the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) separately even though they are not separately explained in the Pāḷi, shows that those foundations of mindfulness should also be explained separately.

The matrices from the Nayamātikā to the Lakkhaṇamātikā are called the 'Dhātukathā Matrix' because they are unique to the Dhātukathā and not common to other texts. The summary of the states to be analyzed, taught within that matrix, is called the 'Abbhantaramātikā' (Internal Matrix). To clarify this meaning, the words beginning with 'Ayañhi' were spoken. In that context, 'without saying so' means without saying it outside of this Dhātukathā matrix, as in 'all matrices... (pe) ... are the matrix'. 'Only within the Dhātukathā' should be understood as 'only within the Dhātukathā matrix'. Because it is placed within the matrix that is unique to that text, it is said to be placed within that very matrix.

Alternatively, the phrase "without stating thus" means not stating it in the way the words "all... the matrix (mātikā)" refer to the mātikā starting from kusalā dhammā and ending with araṇā dhammā, which are external to the Dhātukathā and belong to another treatise (the Dhammasaṅgaṇī). "Only within the Dhātukathā" means it is shown and established in its specific form only within this treatise. Since it is not included (in its specific form) within the mātikā of the entire Abhidhamma (seven books), it should be understood as pakiṇṇaka (miscellaneous) due to its scattered nature.

## 3. Explanation of the Nayamukha Mātikā
The states of inclusion (saṅgaha), non-inclusion (asaṅgaha), dissociation (vippayoga), and association (sampayoga), which serve as the gateways for the occurrence of the methods (naya), are called the "gateways of the methods" (nayamukha). The brief exposition of these gateways is called the Nayamukha Mātikā. The fourteen [methods] of inclusion, non-inclusion, association, and dissociation arise by way of combination; thus, these four are indeed the gateways of the fourteen methods.

In the terms such as "non-included by the included" (saṅgahitena asaṅgahita) within that Nayamukha Mātikā, although inclusion and non-inclusion are taught as far as possible through states like the Truths (sacca), etc., such teaching is done only in the sense of the "includer" (saṅgāhaka) as the agent, not as the "inclusion" (saṅgaha) as the instrument. Furthermore, regarding that inclusion and non-inclusion, in the extraction of states to be questioned and answered, such as "Which states are included by the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) in terms of inclusion by aggregates (khandha-saṅgaha), but not included in terms of inclusion by bases (āyatana-saṅgaha)?", they are taught by being restricted only to the inclusions (as instruments) such as aggregates, etc. Therefore, it is said: "Inclusion by three, non-inclusion by three."

Both in the extraction of states to be questioned and answered and in the questions and answers themselves, the association and dissociation of states starting from the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) up to the araṇa states occur only with the four (mental) aggregates. Therefore, it is said: "Association with four, dissociation with four."

If it is asked: "Does not dissociation also occur with matter (rūpa) and Nibbāna? Why then is it said 'dissociation with four'?"—it is because dissociation that occurs with matter and Nibbāna also occurs only with the four (mental) aggregates. Matter is not dissociated from matter or from Nibbāna, nor is Nibbāna dissociated from matter; they are dissociated only from the four (mental) aggregates. Therefore, the dissociation of the four mental aggregates from matter and Nibbāna is also restricted to the four aggregates that are currently being dissociated, because there can be no dissociation apart from those four aggregates.

That dissociation does not occur for an objectless state (anārammaṇa) with other objectless states or with mixed (missaka) states (those mixed with the objectless). Nor does it occur for a mixed state with objectless states or other mixed states. It should be understood that objectless states and mixed states have dissociation with states that have an object (sārammaṇa); and a state with an object has dissociation with states with an object, objectless states, and mixed states.

## 4. Explanation of the Lakkhaṇa Mātikā
The term "inclusion" (saṅgaha) itself is called the method of inclusion (saṅgaha-naya). This Lakkhaṇa Mātikā term "similar (sabhāga) and dissimilar (visabhāga)" should be contemplated by connecting it separately with the Nayamukha Mātikā term "inclusion by three, non-inclusion by three" and also with the term "association with four, dissociation with four." Because of this separate connection, it should be understood that inclusion and non-inclusion are of the nature of similarity and dissimilarity; likewise, association and dissociation are also (of the nature of similarity and dissimilarity).

Alternatively: For whatever state there is inclusion and non-inclusion, that state is both similar and dissimilar. Likewise, for whatever state there is association and dissociation, that state is also both similar and dissimilar. Between these two explanations, states from the aggregate of matter up to the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) come into the reckoning. In that reckoning, having a common nature such as ruppana (being molested/deformed) is to be understood as similarity (sabhāgatā) in the context of inclusion; and having a common nature such as ekuppāda (arising together) is to be understood as (similarity) in the context of association.

## 5. Explanation of the Bāhira Mātikā
Because it is placed outside the mātikā of the Dhātukathā in this manner, it means being placed behind (the four mātikās) by way of the arrangement: "All the mātikās from the Dhammasaṅgaṇī are also the mātikā of the Dhātukathā." Or, by way of this arrangement, it means that the mātikā terms from kusala states to araṇa states are not directly shown in their specific form here in this Dhātukathā, but the mātikā of another treatise (Dhammasaṅgaṇī), which is external to the Dhātukathā's own mātikā, is established as the mātikā of this treatise; it is so called because it is thus manifested.

Among the terms such as "inclusion (saṅgaha), non-inclusion (asaṅgaha)," etc., why is it said that inclusion is of "four kinds" when it is only of one kind? This is because the word itself is spoken without directly stating the meaning and without yet distinguishing the specific sense. Among the words such as "inclusion, non-inclusion," the meaning here is that the word "inclusion" is of four kinds by the power of its own meaning. Or, there is no fault because the word "inclusion" in "inclusion, non-inclusion," etc., is taken in a general sense where the specific meaning has not yet been distinguished. Only when the specific meaning is distinguished can its one-fold nature exist, not before that (at the general level). Since the word jāti (kind/birth) is a relative term, when it is said "inclusion by kind (jātiyā saṅgaho)," it should be understood as "by its own kind," as no other term suitable for connection is explicitly mentioned. Therefore, "inclusion by kind" (jāti-saṅgaha) mentioned in the section on matter (Rūpakaṇḍa) means "inclusion by its own kind" (sajāti-saṅgaha).

In the Matrix of Methods (Nayamātikā) of this Dhātukathā treatise, these two methods, "Saṅgaho asaṅgaho, sampayogo vippayogo," are summaries (uddesa) that briefly show the method of questioning and answering regarding dhammas in a general sense, without extracting specific dhammas that ought to be questioned or answered. The remaining methods, however, are summaries that extract and show specific dhammas.

Indeed, in the method "Saṅgahitena asaṅgahitaṃ," it should be noted that although it should be stated as "Saṅgahitena asaṅgahitaṃ asaṅgahitaṃ," one word "asaṅgahita" is elided. By that elided word "asaṅgahita," there is a specific non-included dhamma which is distinguished by a specific included dhamma; based on that specific dhamma, the method of questioning and answering, referred to as the state of being non-included, is briefly shown. In the term "saṅgahitena," the instrumental case (karaṇa-vibhatti) should be understood as having the sense of an attribute (visesana). This aforementioned method also applies to the summaries of methods from the third method to the end of the tenth method, excluding the sixth method. In those methods as well, according to the stated method, specific dhammas that ought to be questioned or answered are extracted by two terms each, and the methods of questioning and answering are briefly shown by a third term which is similar to the final term in each respective method. Among those methods, in the fourth and fifth methods, the instrumental case is indicated in the sense of the agent (kattu). In the four methods starting from the seventh, the instrumental case should be understood in the sense of association (sahayoga). It is not in the sense of an attribute having the same locus (samānādhikaraṇa) as in the second and third methods. In those second and third methods, the qualification of one nature by another nature is made; however, in these fourth, fifth, seventh, etc., methods, the qualification of one dhamma by another dhamma is made. In the four methods starting from the eleventh, the specific dhamma is extracted by the initial term alone, and the methods of questioning and answering are briefly shown by the remaining terms. In these methods also, the instrumental case should be understood only in the sense of an attribute. The dhammas which are the basis of questioning and answering distinguish their own state of being associated (sampayutta), dissociated (vippayutta), etc., by means of the qualification such as the state of being included, which acts as the instrument (karaṇa).

"Vikappato" means by way of various arrangements or by way of division. "Sanniṭṭhānavasena" means by way of association with determination (adhimokkha) which has the function of deciding. Here, the meaning should be understood as: by way of association with all arisings of consciousness (cittuppāda) which are taught by way of decision. Adhimokkha is taught by way of association with the arisings of consciousness taught by way of decision; the remaining dhammas are taught by way of association with all arisings of consciousness. Among those dhammas, those such as contact (phassa), which are common to all consciousness (sabbacittasādhāraṇa), are extensive and also prominent; therefore, they should be grasped first. For that reason, the brief indication (uddesa) is made for the purpose of grasping those dhammas, etc., through inclusion. Since uncommon (asādhāraṇa) dhammas should also be grasped, adhimokkha is briefly shown among those uncommon dhammas to demonstrate the inclusion of other dhammas such as initial application (vitakka) by means of adhimokkha, which has a wide range. The phrase "Sanniṭṭhānavasena vuttā" should be understood as being stated with reference to the words in the Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and the Paṭiccasamuppāda-vibhaṅga. Alternatively, in the sense that: there are those dhammas which are taught by way of decision, because of being associated with all those dhammas...
7:
When the common dhammas associated with all consciousness and the uncommon dhammas not so associated are to be taught, among the uncommon dhammas, there is adhimokkha which has a wide range of objects. Because of being associated with all consciousness and mental factors taught by way of that adhimokkha, dhammas such as contact (phassa) are common to all consciousness. Adhimokkha is also taught because it is a dhamma with a wide range of objects among the uncommon dhammas. Since there is no other such dhamma, this meaning should be understood.

In this context, the life faculty (jīvitindriya) should be understood as not being taught because it is mixed with materiality (rūpa). One-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā), however, has a portion that is not of the nature of concentration (samādhi). By the general term (sāmañña-sadda, i.e., the name 'cittekaggatā') and by the general-specific terms (sāmañña-visesa-sadda, such as the faculty of concentration, etc.), cittekaggatā which has the nature of concentration is expressed. There is no other kind of dhamma that ought to be pervaded or excluded which is expressible only by a specific term (visesa-sadda). Because it can show a kind of term that is not a general term pervading other meanings, nor a specific term excluding other meanings, that very dhamma which has the nature of concentration should be expressed by terms such as the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya), which show the distinction. Just as feeling (vedanā) which has the nature of pleasure (sukha), etc., can be expressed by general-specific terms, it should not be expressed by general-specific terms that are the opposite of the stated characteristics. Therefore, when this general term 'cittekaggatā' occurs in a dhamma that does not have the nature of concentration without depending on a specific term, it would itself become a specific term and manifest only the one-pointedness that does not have the nature of concentration. And the other specific term would manifest only the dhamma that has the nature of concentration. Thus, cittekaggatā, which is divided into two kinds, is both uncommon and has a limited range of objects; therefore, it does not deserve to be briefly presented (uddesa) here. Alternatively, even if it is not differentiated, because it is not prominent like contact (phassa), etc., and because it must be expressed depending on other dhammas, that cittekaggatā and jīvitindriya do not deserve to be in the summary (uddesa) and thus are not explicitly shown.

## 2. Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesa)
## 1. First Method: Commentary on the Terms of Inclusion and Non-inclusion
## 1. Commentary on the Term 'Aggregates' (Khandha)
The aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) have been taught as things to be known with higher knowledge (abhiññeyya-dhamma). For the purpose of showing the distinction such as the state of being fully understood (pariññeyyatā) of those things already known with higher knowledge according to their nature, the Truths (sacca) were taught; and for the purpose of showing the distinction of functions such as the state of predominance (adhipati), the faculties (indriya) and so forth were taught. Therefore, just like the distinction of the Truths and so forth, when the distinction of inclusion (saṅgaha) and non-inclusion (asaṅgaha) is taught based on things to be known with higher knowledge, it becomes easily understood. Thus, it should be understood that the Mātikā (Matrix), which is the beginning of the method, was established as: "Inclusion is by three; non-inclusion is by three."

Because of this, association (sampayoga) and dissociation (vippayoga), which are taught as being "by four," were also questioned and answered by means of the aggregates and so forth, based on things to be known with higher knowledge.

In the Pali text, "The aggregate of matter is included by one aggregate," those things which are taught as "the aggregate of matter" (rūpakkhandha) have a common nature (sabhāgatā) as the aggregate of matter among the five aggregates. Therefore, the inclusion or counting is shown either by the counting known as the state of being the aggregate of matter, or by the counting known as the term "aggregate of matter." Therefore, He said "yañhi kiñci" and so forth. By the term "rūpakkhandha," the thing to be included or counted is shown. The expression "by one aggregate" shows the inclusion by which meaning it is included. The meaning here is that it is counted by one aggregate-count among the five aggregate-counts. Since inclusion is taught by terms such as aggregates, He will later say "included by the inclusion of aggregates" (khandhasaṅgahena saṅgahitā) and so forth.

The phrase "Asaṅgahanayaniddese" is spoken as a part of this very method "Saṅgaho Asaṅgaho," and should not be understood as a different method. By this statement that only the dyads (duka), triads (tika), and tetrads (catukka) with the aggregate of matter as the root (mūla) are shown here, it is shown that because there is no difference in meaning when things with the aggregate of feeling as the root are combined with the previously mentioned aggregate of matter, one obtains 3 dyads, 2 triads, and 1 tetrad by combining only with the subsequent aggregate of perception and so forth; 2 dyads and 1 triad with the aggregate of perception as the root; and 1 dyad with the aggregate of formations as the root. It should be noted that the questions and answers made immediately after the fivefold group of questions and answers according to their divisions are summarized; or it should be noted that they are not included in the Pali text because they can be understood by the method already stated.

## Commentary on the Terms of Bases (Āyatana) and so forth
In the phrase "Yasmā ca dukatikesu," although the answer (vissajjana) is the same in the singles (ekaka) as well, while the answers for the eye-faculty, ear-faculty, pleasure-faculty, etc., are the same in the singles, different answers are seen in the dyads and so forth. In this Exposition of Faculties (Indriya-niddesa), just as one does not find identical answers between the eye-ear dyad and the eye-pleasure-faculty dyad, one also does not find the answers of the dyads and triads to be the same. However, in this Exposition of Truths (Sacca-niddesa), the answers for the suffering-origination dyad and the suffering-path dyad are found to be identical to each other and to the triad. Therefore, the fact that the answers are identical only in the dyads and triads is given as the reason for teaching the Truth of the Path immediately after the Truth of Origination.

## 6. Commentary on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda)
Although it should be written without starting a new question as "Ignorance is included by one aggregate; with ignorance as condition, formations are included by one aggregate," it should be understood that due to oversight, this phrase "Ignorance is included by one aggregate" was not written. Or else, it should be understood that by using the single term "ignorance" as a word-retention (sarūpekasesa), the answer for ignorance is shown. In this context of "all resultant consciousness" (sabbampi vipākaviññāṇaṃ), it should not be qualified by the word "resultant" (vipāka). This is because consciousness such as wholesome (kusala) and so forth are also included in the Dhātukathā by terms such as "with formations as condition, consciousness." In the Exposition of Terms on Inclusion and Non-inclusion by Dissociation, those types of consciousness are shown with an answer different from the answer for the term "resultant states" (vipākā dhammā). In this Exposition of Terms on Inclusion and Non-inclusion, since it is stated that mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) is included by 11 bases, it can be known that non-kamma-born states are also included.

Because they are merely the states of arising, maturing, and breaking up of things that are arising, maturing, and breaking up, birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa) cannot be separated as distinct ultimate realities (paramattha), but are merely the nature of ultimate things. Since those instances of birth, aging, and death are the moments of arising, maturing, and breaking up of matter, they are taken by the nature of being molested (ruppana) and thus share a common nature with the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). However, the moments of arising and so forth of mental states, just like the birth etc. of material clusters (rūpa-kalāpa), occur individually due to the state of arising etc. of the group of four mental aggregates that arise together. They are not taken by the definite ultimate functions of feeling, perceiving, or cognizing, but are taken by the non-definite ultimate function of constructing conditioned things (saṅkhata-abhisaṅkharaṇa); therefore, they share a common nature with the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Likewise, both types of birth, aging, and death are not taken by definite ultimate functions like the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) etc., but share a common nature with the mental-base (dhammāyatana) and the mental-element (dhammadhātu) due to the meaning of being non-substantial (nissatta). Because they share a common nature with the aggregates and so forth in this way, He said: "Birth is included by two aggregates," and so forth.

## The Commentary on the Terms of Inclusion and Non-inclusion of the First Method is finished.

## 2. Second Method: Explanation of the Section on Included and Non-included

In the description of the section on 'Included and Non-included' (saṅgahitenāsaṅgahitapada), those dhammas which are to be questioned and answered as non-included (asaṅgahita), but are specifically distinguished as being included (saṅgahita), are extracted. Desiring to show those very dhammas first, the Buddha said: "By the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), which dhammas are included by way of aggregate-inclusion (khandhasaṅgaha) but not included by way of base-inclusion (āyatanasaṅgaha) or element-inclusion (dhātusaṅgaha)?" In all methods, the general inclusions by aggregates etc. always depend on specific distinctions, and because the questions and answers rely on differences, the counting of aggregates etc. is specific and not merely general.

In this second method, since the specific dhamma has already been extracted by the mere words 'included and non-included', it would be sufficient to show those dhammas which are included by one or two of the three types of inclusion but not by the others, using only the phrase 'included by aggregate-inclusion, not included by base or element inclusion'. However, because such dhammas [that fit only that description without further specification] are not possible, and because the Method-Matrix (nayamātikā) depends on the Internal Matrix (abbhantaramātikā) and External Matrix (bāhiramātikā), and since it is known in the summary (uddesa) that the 'included and non-included' is extracted in relation to whichever dhamma—from the matter-aggregate (rūpakkhandha) to the 'without-war' (araṇa) dhammas—acts as the includer (agent), the phrase 'By the eye-base' etc. is stated to define and show the dhamma extracted by that specific includer. In methods where there is no extraction of a specific dhamma to be questioned and answered, such as in the first and sixth methods, the dhammas from the matter-aggregate to the 'without-war' dhammas are pointed out as the subjects to be questioned and answered; in other methods, they are pointed out as the defining factors of the extracted dhammas.

In this second method, in the terms 'By the eye-base... by the touch-element (phoṭṭhabbadhātu)', the instrumental case should be understood as expressing the sense of the agent (kattu). In the terms 'by aggregate-inclusion, by base-inclusion, by element-inclusion', it is in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa). Here, whichever agent of inclusion is used, if there is another dhamma among the inclusions of aggregates etc. that should or should not be included by that specific inclusion, that dhamma alone is extracted as the included or non-included. There is no other dhamma that should be included by aggregate-inclusion through the matter-aggregate (rūpakkhandha); the same applies to the feeling-aggregate (vedanākkhandha) and so on. A dhamma itself cannot be its own includer or non-includer. The statement 'The matter-aggregate is included by one aggregate' is not meant to imply that the matter-aggregate is included by itself; rather, it has been explained that it refers to being included by virtue of being the matter-aggregate or by the term 'matter-aggregate'.

If a dhamma were to be included by itself, then in the description of the section on 'Associated and Dissociated with the Included', it would have been stated starting with: 'By the feeling-aggregate, those dhammas which are included by aggregate-inclusion...'
