...included by base-inclusion, included by element-inclusion, those dhammas are associated with 3 aggregates, 1 base, and 7 elements,' and so on. But it was not so stated. Therefore, just as consciousness (citta) is not associated or dissociated with itself, so the matter-aggregate (rūpakkhandha) is not included or non-included by the matter-aggregate itself. The same applies to the feeling-aggregate and others. This is because a dhamma itself is not its own similar (sabhāga) or dissimilar (visabhāga) part.

For this reason, just as parts cannot be the includer or non-includer of the whole, the whole cannot be the includer or non-includer of the parts. For example, the matter-aggregate cannot be the includer or non-includer of the eye-base etc.; the mental-object base (dhammāyatana) cannot be the includer or non-includer of the feeling-aggregate etc.; and the 'without-war' (araṇa) dhammas cannot be the includer or non-includer of the four aggregates. This is because there is no distinction within the parts contained in a whole that could make them similar or dissimilar to the whole. Likewise, the whole cannot be the includer or non-includer of those things that are similar or dissimilar to the parts.

For example, the mental-object base (dhammāyatana) cannot be the includer or non-includer, by way of aggregate-inclusion, of a part of the matter-aggregate (gross matter) which is similar to subtle matter (sukhumarūpa) but dissimilar to feeling etc. The life-faculty (jīvitindriya) also cannot be the includer or non-includer, by aggregate-inclusion alone, of the parts of the matter-aggregate and the formations-aggregate (saṅkhārakkhandha) which are similar or dissimilar to the physical and mental life-faculties. A dhamma that is similar to a part is not necessarily similar to the whole, nor is a dhamma that is dissimilar to a part necessarily dissimilar to the whole.

Therefore, even if there is a non-includer state regarding a dhamma other than itself, or other than what is included within itself, or other than what is similar to its own part, since there is no 'includer-ness' (saṅgāhakatā) in those dhammas, they cannot be non-includers of what is already included. Because of this lack of 'includer-ness', it should be understood that such dhammas are not taken in the second method.

Statements such as 'The mental-object base, excluding the unconditioned, is included by 4 aggregates' and 'The eye-base and ear-base are included by 1 aggregate' do not show the parts including the whole or the whole including the parts. Rather, they show the fivefold distinction of the mental-object base according to whether it can or cannot be counted by the fourfold aggregate-counting, and the single nature of the eye-base etc. according to their being countable by the single aggregate-counting.

Since the first method merely shows the counting of dhammas that can or cannot be counted by various countings without regard to the includer or non-includer, it is a method consisting only of the object (kamma) and the instrument (karaṇa). The second method and others, however, show the non-counting etc. of dhammas included or not included by includers or non-includers; thus, they are methods consisting of all three: agent (kattu), instrument (karaṇa), and object (kamma). Similarly, in the first method, the presence or absence of the respective aggregates etc., known as the state of being countable or uncountable in various ways, constitutes the state of being similar (sabhāga) or dissimilar (visabhāga).
12:
Similarity (sabhāgatā) and dissimilarity (visabhāgatā) mean that in the Second Method and others, when showing the states that have been extracted, similarity is the state of being the same in terms of aggregates and so on between the includer (saṅgāhaka) and the states to be included (saṅgahetabba), while the absence of such similarity is dissimilarity. In the questions and answers, the presence or absence of those respective aggregates and so on is indeed similarity and dissimilarity; this point is the distinction between the First Method and the Second Method, etc.

Regarding terms similar to the Truth of Origin (samudaya sacca) and the Faculty of Pleasure (sukhindriya), there are only states to be included by those terms. Since there are no states that, having been included [by aggregate], are not included by bases and elements (i.e., because there is no state of being a non-includer), those terms are not extracted.

Terms similar to the Truth of Suffering (dukkha sacca) are a collection of dissimilar states and are endowed with many aggregates; thus, there are no states to be included by aggregate, nor are there states not included by other bases and elements. Thus, because of the absence of both the state of being an includer and the state of being a non-includer, [the Truth of Suffering is also not extracted].

It should be understood that because of this absence of the state of being an includer, the absence of the state of being a non-includer, or the absence of both, terms similar to the aforementioned form aggregate (rūpakkhandha) and so on are not extracted; rather, only terms such as the eye base (cakkhāyatana) are extracted because they possess both the state of being an includer and the state of being a non-includer. In that Second Method, when it is said, "Which states are included by the eye base through aggregate-inclusion?", it should be understood that the physical states (rūpa-dhamma) excluding the eye base itself are included by aggregate; it does not mean the entire form aggregate is included. It has already been shown that the eye base, being a part, cannot include the form aggregate, which is the whole.

In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, the meaning of the term "khandhapadena" is "by the group of aggregates which is the cause of inclusion"; it does not mean "by the aggregate which is the includer." Nevertheless, it is stated by bringing in the subject "a certain includer such as the eye base." That answer means it is not appropriate for includers such as the form aggregate. If one asks: "By the form aggregate, only the form aggregate is included; and there is no such thing as a form aggregate that is not included by the eleven bases and elements. By this method, the eye base includes only the form aggregate, and since there is no state not included by bases and elements, shouldn't it follow that the eye base and so on should also not be taken in this method?"

Such a fault does not occur. The reason is that the meaning of the word "eva" (only) in the phrase "rūpakkhandha-va" (only the form aggregate) does not exclude states other than the form aggregate, but rather excludes states other than the includer itself. The phrase "so ca" (and that) and so on is not an independent statement but is a statement dependent on the includer. How? Just as there are states other than the eye base included by aggregate through the eye base, and those states might be not included by bases and elements; but by the form aggregate, there are no states other than the form aggregate included by aggregate. The intention here is only that "by the form aggregate, only the form aggregate is included through aggregate-inclusion." The view might arise: "Let that very form aggregate be not included by bases and elements through the form aggregate." Wishing to prevent that view, it is said: "And that form aggregate is not such a thing as a form aggregate not included by the eleven bases and elements..."
13:
...when it is said "there is not," here the term "by the form aggregate" (rūpakkhandhena) should be brought in and stated. In saying so, it is appropriate to say that the absence of the state of being not included is stated by this figurative method (pariyāya): that the form aggregate is neither an includer nor a non-includer of the form aggregate itself or its parts such as the eye base through inclusion by bases and elements. It is not appropriate to say [there is an absence of the state of being not included] because the form aggregate or its parts are included by the eleven bases and elements through the form aggregate. For such a state of being included does not exist. If it did exist, the form aggregate should also be extracted in the exposition of the section "Inclusion of the Associated and Dissociated" (Saṅgahatena Sampayutta Vippayutta). For if it were extracted, the form aggregate or its parts would be included by the three types of inclusion, and those states also have the quality of being dissociated (vippayutta).

In the statement "Because of the absence of the state of being not included, these and other [terms are not taken]," the meaning is: just as with the eye base and so on, these terms like the form aggregate and others are not taken as includers (saṅgāhaka) because there is no absence of the state of being not included among the states they include, or because there is no appropriate answer as there is for the eye base.

In that Commentary, the statement "By the form aggregate, only the form aggregate is included" is refuted by showing the absence of both the state of being included and the state of being not included for that very form aggregate. The reason given here for not taking [certain terms], which is understood as "because of the absence of the state of being not included even though there is inclusion," would be appropriate for the Truth of Origin (samudaya sacca) and so on, because there is no absence of the state of being not included among the states included by those Truths of Origin. But for the form aggregate and so on, there is no state included at all; how then could there be a state of being not included for it? Therefore, the reason for not taking them here is simply the absence of the state of being an includer (saṅgāhaka).

Although the state of being not included through the absence of the state of being included does not exist for the form aggregate etc. in relation to itself, or its internal parts like the eye base, or states similar to its parts, it does exist for other states. Therefore, the absence of both, as in the case of the Truth of Suffering (dukkha sacca) etc., is not appropriate to be the reason for not taking them here. Since the Dhamma base (dhammāyatana), the life faculty (jīvitindriya), etc., possess the state of being includers of the four aggregates, two aggregates, etc., and it is not that there is no absence of the state of being not included by bases and elements for those included states by the Dhamma base, life faculty, etc. (i.e., there is such an absence), the reason "absence of the state of being not included" is inconclusive (anekantika). Therefore, the reason for not taking the terms that are not taken, and for taking the terms that are taken, should be understood only by the method previously stated.

In the phrase "Anidassanaṃ punadeva sappaṭighaṃ," by this term "anidassanaṃ," connecting it with the word "sappaṭigha" mentioned in the term "sanidassana-sappaṭighaṃ"...
14:
The invisible-impinging (anidassana-sappaṭigha) states have been shown. Again, with the word 'puna deva', by turning back and taking the visible (sanidassana) term which remained in that very 'visible-impinging' (sanidassana-sappaṭigha) term, the 'visible-dyad' (sanidassana-duka) term is shown. It is not possible to say, 'By the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), only the eye-base itself is included.' Because it should not be said that 'By the eye-base, the eye-base is included by way of inclusion of bases (āyatana-sangaha)' nor 'it is not included'; thus this method is shown. In this way, in all sections, whether it be the whole group of those states or a part of that group, the fact that it should not be so stated should be applied to the words 'the including state is included' and 'the non-including state is not included'. Indeed, it is only because of the absence of the state of being a non-includer that the eye-base etc. are not said to be 'not included' by the eye-base etc., and not because of the absence of the state of being an includer.

## The explanation of the second method: inclusion by what is included and exclusion (sangahitena-asangahita) is finished.

## 3. The Third Method: Explanation of the term 'Inclusion by what is excluded' (asangahitena-sangahita)

In the description of the term 'inclusion by what is excluded' (asangahitena-sangahita), although the three aggregates such as feeling (vedanā) etc. and Nibbāna, which are not included by the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) through the inclusion of aggregates (khandha-sangaha), have a common nature with subtle matter (sukhumarūpa) by way of base (āyatana) and element (dhātu), yet because subtle matter alone is not the aggregate of matter, there is no common nature of base and element with the aggregate of matter. Therefore, those states such as feeling etc. are not included by that aggregate of matter through the inclusions of base and element. It is not that those states are not only not included by that [aggregate of matter] through those inclusions, but they are also not 'not included'. This is because they have a common nature by way of base and element with subtle matter, which is a part of that aggregate of matter. However, in this third method, only the absence of the state of being included is intended. Those states which are not included by the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), eye-base (cakkhāyatana), etc., are not included by those [consciousness aggregate etc.] in every way, because they are not mixed in any way with those consciousness aggregate etc. The truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) etc., which are the collection of the five aggregates, also do not include Nibbāna—which is not included by the inclusion of aggregates—through the inclusions of base and element, just like the aggregate of matter. Therefore, it should be known that such states are not taken as 'non-includers' only because of the absence of the state of being an includer. But in the case of indeterminate states (abyākatadhamma) etc., which are the collection of the five aggregates along with Nibbāna, it is precisely because of the absence of the state of being a non-includer. For there is no state which they cannot include by the inclusion of aggregates. Neither oneself, nor a part of oneself, nor a state that has a common nature with a part of oneself, is 'not included' by oneself. As for the aggregates of feeling etc., they are taken in this third method because of the fact that they include by way of bases those states which are not included by themselves by way of aggregates.
15:
The statement in the Commentary, 'Those states which are included by the mind-base (dhammāyatana),' should not be said (here). Because there is no state that is not included by the mind-base through any kind of inclusion. Since the mind-base is a collection of the four dissimilar aggregates and Nibbāna, it does not include itself by way of inclusion of aggregates; and also because of the absence of the state of being an includer through the inclusions of base and element, this method is shown. Therefore, the meaning of this statement is that they are counted by the counting of the mind-base. By the Pali 'Yāni... pe... gahitāni', it shows that: terms such as the bases of power (iddhipāda) etc. which show a part of the mind-base mixed with consciousness; terms such as the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) etc. which show a part of the mind-base mixed with gross matter (oḷārikarūpa); terms such as the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), eye-base (cakkhāyatana) etc. which do not show the mind-base at all; and terms such as the mind-base (dhammāyatana) etc. which show the entire mind-base—excluding these, the terms which show a part of the mind-base not mixed with other bases are taken.

## The explanation of the third method: inclusion by what is excluded (asangahitena-sangahita) is finished.

## 4. The Fourth Method: Explanation of the term 'Inclusion by what is included' (sangahitena-sangahita)

In the description of the term 'inclusion by what is included' (sangahitena-sangahita), just as the second and third methods were presented as 'exclusion by what is included' (sangahitena-asangahita) and 'inclusion by what is excluded' (asangahitena-sangahita) through the distinction of the occurrence of inclusion and non-inclusion of the three inclusions (aggregates, bases, elements), the fourth and fifth methods are not so. The fourth method is presented as 'inclusion by what is included' (sangahitena-sangahita) only by the occurrence of inclusion. The fifth method is presented as 'exclusion by what is excluded' (asangahitena-asangahita) only by the occurrence of non-inclusion. Therefore, these two methods depend on the distinction of included states and excluded states, apart from the distinction of the occurrence of inclusion. In this fourth method, a specific state included by a certain state should be questioned and answered as being a specific state included again by the state of being included. Desiring to show first that very determined state, he said: 'By the truth of the origin (samudayasacca), those states which are included by aggregate... pe... are included; by those states, those states which are included by aggregate... pe... are included.'

In this fourth method, states that cannot be included by all three—aggregate, base, and element—such as the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha), aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), mind-base (dhammāyatana), truth of suffering (dukkhasacca), etc.; states that cannot be included by the two—base and element—such as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) etc.; states that cannot be included by only one—aggregate—such as the aggregate of feeling (vedanā), truth of cessation (nirodhasacca), life-faculty (jīvitindriya), etc., or by only one—element—such as the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu) etc., are not extracted as includers because of the absence of the state of being an includer. By the three...
16:
Those phenomena that can be included by the three—aggregates, bases, and elements—which are the means of inclusion, are presented here in this Fourth Method because of the absence of the absence of the ability to include (meaning, because they can be included by all three). Indeed, those phenomena such as the four mental aggregates (saṅkhārakkhandha, etc.) included by these three inclusions also certainly include in return those phenomena such as the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca) which include them. Only the inclusion (saṅgaha) of those phenomena should be questioned and answered again.

In the Commentary, however, by the term "sakale na khandhādipadena," it should be understood as the word that expresses the whole, such as the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). Regarding the statement, "Having included the phenomenon that includes itself, it should again reach inclusion by that very phenomenon," it cannot be said that "there is no other included (saṅgahita) besides that" without connecting it with the word "aggregate" and so on. This is because it is not the inclusion of that very phenomenon by which it was included that is questioned and answered, nor is it only that phenomenon itself; rather, it is only the inclusion of the phenomenon included by that [first] phenomenon that is questioned and answered.

Just as feeling (vedanā) is an aggregate and sound (sadda) is a base, subtle matter (sukhuma-rūpa) is not like that. That subtle matter is only a portion of the aggregates and bases. Therefore, instead of saying "a portion of subtle matter" (sukhumarupekadesaṃ vā), it is said as "subtle matter" (sukhuma-rūpaṃ vā). In all sentences, it should be connected as "unmixed with other phenomena." Also, the statement, "With reference to those phenomena which are included by those very phenomena by way of aggregates etc.," cannot be said in that way. This is because it is not the inclusion of the included by the included that is questioned and answered here, but rather the inclusion itself. Therefore, here, in "ekena khandhena," this meaning "by one counting of aggregate" is the only correct one; it does not mean "by the agent that includes." This is because one aggregate does not include a portion of itself.

## စတုတ္ထနယသင်္ဂဟိတေနသင်္ဂဟိတပဒဝဏ္ဏနာ နိဋ္ဌိတာ။

## ၅။ ပဉ္စမနယော အသင်္ဂဟိတေနအသင်္ဂဟိတပဒဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the exposition of the terms "Not Included by the Not Included" (asaṅgahitena asaṅgahita) as well, the presentation of the phenomena determined and extracted in the Pāḷi should be understood according to the method already stated. Here, the groups of phenomena associated with consciousness taken together with subtle matter are similar to the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), non-apparent and non-impinging phenomena (anidassana-appaṭigha), non-mental phenomena (acetasika), and non-clung-to phenomena (anupādā). Even if some phenomena cannot be included by one or two inclusions, they are not phenomena that cannot be included by a complete inclusion because there is no phenomenon that should not be included by all three inclusions. Phenomena similar to indeterminate phenomena (abyākata-dhamma) are also not phenomena that cannot be included because there is no nature that should not be included by any inclusion. Therefore, those phenomena are not extracted as being "not includable," but the remaining phenomena such as the aggregate of matter are extracted because they are the opposite of that.
17:
In the Commentary, the statement "By such a term, Nibbāna would not reach the state of being counted as an aggregate" is said with reference to the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). Among the non-including terms (asaṅgāhaka) in the non-apparent and non-impinging (anidassana-appaṭigha) terms, Nibbāna is included within. Yet, that Nibbāna itself is not the non-includer of that Nibbāna. All the problems, such as the first problem, the problem of mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa), etc., together with the second problem etc. made by combining those with similar answers, are thirty-four. By the phrase "that very term" (tadeva) which is extracted in the question, it refers to the specific term such as the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). It does not refer to the phenomena to be questioned that are specifically determined. This is because those phenomena to be questioned are shown only by their characteristics, not by their specific form through the term.

In that term "tadeva," by the word "eva" (only/certainly), it should be understood that it shows the certainty of the state of being "not included by the not included" only for the extracted term, and the uncertainty for other non-extracted terms, implying that the term is never not "not included by the not included." In the phrase "tadeva yehi asaṅgahitaṃ," the remaining word "niyamato" (by rule/certainly) can be connected. Alternatively, in "tadeva," the word "eva" has the meaning of strictly defining the state of being "not included by the not included" only for the term extracted in the question. It should be regarded as not having the meaning of prohibiting the state of being "not included by the not included" for other non-extracted phenomena. For the term extracted in the question, whether it is with other phenomena or without other phenomena, it is "not included by the not included." For instance, the aggregate of matter etc. are with other phenomena, while the aggregate of consciousness etc. are without other phenomena.

The statement "the remaining phenomena are included" (avasesā saṅgahitā) should be regarded as "the remaining phenomena are not 'not included'." The meaning is that those material phenomena are "not included" by those consciousness phenomena by way of the three inclusions; thus, being extracted in the question, they become non-includers by the three inclusions and are "not included." Even the non-extracted phenomena such as feeling (vedanā) etc. are indeed "not included." Here, in the first method, it is said that feeling etc. are also "not included" by consciousness. In the second method, only material phenomena are mentioned. This is the distinction between the two methods. When it is said that feeling etc. are "not included" by way of inclusions such as aggregates only by matter and consciousness, it means they are "not included" by the three inclusions by way of gross matter (oḷārika-rūpa) and consciousness. This is because here, by the taking of "matter" (rūpa), gross matter, which is a portion of matter, is taken.

In the fourth problem, in the phrase "the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) by the four such as feeling etc.," it should be regarded that by this term "eye-base," the non-includer (asaṅgāhaka) extracted in the question is shown. The phenomena not included by the eye-base (and not included by the consciousness aggregate) are the ten gross bases (oḷārikāyatana). It is not only the eye-base itself. By the verse beginning with "rūpañca dhammāyatanaṃ," those phenomena which are not included by the three inclusions are only consciousness. By the not included...
18:
By that very verse, all states excluding consciousness, which are not included by that [consciousness], are shown in brief. Indeed, states with similar answers should be shown together in brief. Among those states with similar answers, when those similar to the first, the rūpakkhandha, have been shown together in brief, other states with dissimilar answers are shown by way of providing the method. Therefore, it is said: "Rūpa and dhammāyatana... and so on, are shown in brief by another way." In that verse, "two existences" (dve bhavā) refers to the non-percipient existence (asaññasatta-bhava) and the one-constituent existence (ekavokāra-bhava). The word "two" (dve) is mentioned with reference only to external states (bāhira-dhamma) and derived states (upādā-dhamma). That state, such as rūpakkhandha, which is not an includer and by which the non-included states like viññāṇakkhandha are defined in terms of what is to be questioned and answered, is called the "subject matter" (visaya) because it is the basis for the non-included states and for the questions and answers. Because it is merely the giving of the method for the summary verse (uddāna) as shown, it is called the "method" (naya). There is also a reading "dvevīsanayo ca," which means this method has twenty-two terms.

## The explanation of the fifth method: Not included by the not-included, is finished.

## 6. The explanation of the sixth method: The terms of association and dissociation

Regarding the terms of association (sampayoga) and dissociation (vippayoga), the statement "all that is obtained and all that is not obtained is taken in the question" should be understood as referring not to terms such as rūpakkhandha, but only to the terms "association" and "dissociation." Indeed, among the rūpakkhandha and so on, whatever term such as dhammāyatana is not obtained, that term is also not taken in the question. However, although the term "association" is not obtained in rūpakkhandha and so on, it is taken in the question thus: "With how many... is the rūpakkhandha associated?" It is obtained in vedanākkhandha and so on. As for the term "dissociation," it is obtained in all terms such as rūpakkhandha and is thus taken in the question. For material states (rūpa-dhamma), there is no such thing as association with matter or with Nibbāna; nor is there association of Nibbāna with matter. Thus, the commentator, in denying association due to the absence of the common nature of arising together (ekuppāda) and so on, should be understood as also denying dissociation, because the very [absence of] arising together is the dissimilar nature (visabhāga) of these states, and due to the absence of that common nature, dissociation is also denied. Indeed, the existence of arising together and so on in the four mental aggregates (nāma-khandha) constitutes their mutual similarity (sabhāga). There is a dissimilarity (visabhāga) between those mental aggregates and matter/Nibbāna, and between matter/Nibbāna and those mental aggregates. But that arising together and so on, which would constitute the dissimilarity between one part of matter and another part of matter or Nibbāna, or between Nibbāna and matter, does not exist in a part of matter or in Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said: "There is dissociation from the four mental aggregates."
19:
Regarding the states that are not dissociated from even one of the seven consciousness elements (viññāṇadhātu)—this does not mean showing states mixed with objectless matter, such as the fine-material existence (rūpabhava) being dissociated from three consciousness elements, or states that are neither resultant nor giving result (nevavipākanavipākadhamma) being dissociated from five consciousness elements, or states without initial and sustained application (avitakka-avicāra) being dissociated from one consciousness element. Rather, it intends to show those states that are associated with all seven consciousness elements if they are not dissociated from even one, or to show those seven consciousness elements themselves. "Avippayutta" (not dissociated) means those states that are not dissociated, and it does not mean those that are associated (sampayutta). Therefore, it means not to take all those states mixed with objectless matter and Nibbāna, such as the terms dhammāyatana etc. which show what is associated with those consciousness elements, the terms acetasika etc. which show what cannot be said to be associated or dissociated, and the terms dukkha-sacca etc. which show what is associated and what cannot be said. This is because all the seven consciousness elements mixed with objectless matter and Nibbāna, and the group of both those consciousness elements and their associated states, do not have association or dissociation with anything among the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).

If there is no dissociation in these states mixed with objectless states, then in the explanation of the tenth method (vippayuttena-vippayutta), should it not be said: "Those states which are dissociated from states that are dissociated from wholesome states"? This is because unwholesome and indeterminate states are both types of states mixed with objectless matter and Nibbāna. This is not so. It is because the statement about the absence of association and dissociation for the aforementioned groups refers only to their relation with the aggregates etc. The aggregates etc. are parts of that group, or are groups of other parts like rūpakkhandha etc. Since there is no division between the whole and its parts, there is no similarity (sabhāga) or dissimilarity (visabhāga). Therefore, those states do not have association or dissociation with the aggregates etc. However, wholesome states (kusala) are already distinct from unwholesome (akusala) and indeterminate (abyākata) states. Those unwholesome and indeterminate states are also distinct from wholesome states. There is no relationship of whole and part between them. Therefore, when showing only the fact of dissociation without considering the aggregates etc., wholesome states and other states, and other states and wholesome states, are said to be mutually dissociated because of the existence of dissimilarity (visabhāga). This method applies to all such instances.

In the summary verse (uddāna), the phrase "eighteen, and after that" should be said as "sixteen." The word "twenty-three" should also be said as "twenty-one." In all problems, the parts of the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), the mind-object base (dhammāyatana), and the mind-object element (dhammadhātu), which are the collection of many states whether free or not free from the distinctions of time and continuity—such as the truth of origin (samudaya-sacca), the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), etc.; the bases of power (iddhipāda) etc. which are mixed with parts; the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) etc. which are not mixed with objectless states; and those not mixed with states having objects...
20:
In this context, only those states that possess the same time and continuity and are distinguished by specific parts are taken according to the conditions of being associated (sampayutta) and dissociated (vippayutta). These states, distinguished by specific parts, obtain the state of association and dissociation as appropriate. This is because there exists in those states similarity (sabhāga), such as arising together, and dissimilarity (visabhāga). Therefore, in various Pāḷi texts, it is stated: "associated with some by one aggregate, one base, and one element," and "dissociated from some by one base and one element."

However, the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), and the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) are merely collections of parts belonging to different times. When occurring in the present, they are only individual states. Therefore, since there are no states to be distinguished at the same time within those aggregates, the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) and so on cannot divide the aggregate of feeling. The eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu) and so on also cannot divide the aggregate of consciousness and the mind-base (manāyatana). For this reason, it is not stated that "the faculty of pleasure is dissociated from some by one aggregate," or "the eye-consciousness element is dissociated from some by one aggregate and one base," and so forth. Nevertheless, although there is no division by aggregate and base, consciousness is indeed stated as divided by element; thus it is said, "the eye-consciousness element... up to... the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) is dissociated from sixteen elements." In this same way, regarding the faculty of pleasure and so on which are divided by faculty, dissociation should be understood as appropriate in such phrases as "those states which are dissociated from the faculty of pleasure," but not for the undivided aggregate of feeling.

If it is asked: "Just as it is stated that the Truth of Origin (samudaya-sacca) is associated with three aggregates with reference to its state of association, why is it not stated that it is dissociated from three aggregates with reference to its state of dissociation?"—it is because it is inappropriate to speak of dissociation with those undivided aggregates. If there were division, it would be appropriate to say that the Truth of Origin is dissociated from the faculties of pleasure, pain, and grief (sukha, dukkha, domanassindriya), and from consciousness elements other than the mind-consciousness element. This is because dissimilarity is already included by the very fact of division. However, it is not appropriate to speak of dissociation with the undivided aggregate of feeling and so on. This is because there is no state of dissimilarity between the existing Truth of Origin and those existing aggregates of feeling and so on.

Unlike future states which are not considered by the distinction of time, the conditioned states (saṅkhata) extracted in this method are extracted as associated or dissociated states based on their present status. Such extraction occurs because of the existence of undivided conditioned aggregates and so on, based solely on their present status. There is no association of a non-existent state with a non-existent state, of a non-existent state with an existent state, or of an existent state with a non-existent state. In the case of dissociation, however, if the distinction indicating non-existence is taken, dissimilarity is also taken by that very fact.
21:
If the distinction (bheda) indicating non-existence is not taken, because the state of dissimilarity (visabhāga) is not taken by those various Pali passages, and because the nature of things can be delimited by existence when similarity (sabhāga) exists, existence is shown. Therefore, similarity, known as the state of arising together (ekuppāda), etc., is also taken. Because that similarity is taken, only association (sampayutta) is obtained, not dissociation (vippayoga). Therefore, the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca) is stated as being associated with the aggregate of feeling, etc., not as being dissociated. This method applies to the Truth of the Path (maggasacca), etc., as well.

“Excluding the sustained application (vicāra) of the second jhāna, the remaining are states with sustained application only (avitakka-vicāramatta)”: This commentary statement shows that only those prominent states which, like initial application (vitakka), are not submerged in other constituent mental arisings are intended here as states with sustained application only (avitakka-vicāramatta). Because initial application (vitakka) is not taken, in the seventh method, they have the same course as the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca). Since they do not have the same course as states with both initial and sustained application (savitakka-savicāra), those states are not taken. From the tenth to the final fourteenth method, the dissociation of those dissociated from those [states] and the dissociation from the sixteen elements (dhātu) and inclusion (sangahita) in the eighteen elements are stated.

Even if those states with sustained application only (avitakka-vicāramatta) together with initial application (vitakka) are taken, all those states are associated with sustained application (vicāra). Therefore, it is possible to say “associated with some states by one aggregate.” That group of states cannot be associated with any other state excluding sustained application (vicāra). The association of initial application (vitakka), which is a part of that group of states with sustained application only (avitakka-vicāramatta), with a state other than sustained application (vicāra) is not the association of the whole group (samudāya). Just as the association of the base of power of desire (chandiddhipāda), etc., which are parts of the group of four bases of power (iddhipāda) arising in various mental arisings, with the three aggregates is not the association of the group of bases of power, so it should be understood here.

However, among those four bases of power (iddhipāda), there is no single base of power that is not associated (asampayutta) with the aggregates of feeling and perception and a part of the aggregate of mental formations. Thus, the association of the group of bases of power with those aggregates is stated. Similarly, in this case of states with sustained application only (avitakka-vicāramatta), since there is no part of the states with sustained application only that is not associated with sustained application (vicāra), it is not that the association of the group with that sustained application cannot be stated (it can be stated). It is not that the association of states with sustained application only (avitakka-vicāramatta) should not be stated like the states having roots to be abandoned by vision (dassanena-pahātabba-hetuka), etc. (it should be stated). Among the states having roots to be abandoned by vision, some are associated with delusion (moha), which is a part of the aggregate of mental formations, and some are not; thus the group is not associated with that delusion. Since there is no other root state with which that group can be associated, it is stated: “There are no states associated with states having roots to be abandoned by vision.” The same applies to states having roots to be abandoned by development (bhāvanāya-pahātabba-hetuka) and states with roots (sahetuka), etc. But in this case of states with sustained application only (avitakka-vicāramatta), it is not so. It is not that the sustained application (vicāra) with which the group of states with sustained application only would be associated does not exist (it does exist). This is because there is no part among the states with sustained application only that is not associated with sustained application (vicāra).
22:
Because there is no state that is not associated with sustained thought (vicāra), it is not that those states of 'sustained thought only' (avitakkavicāramatta) should not be called 'associated states' (they indeed should be). In all problems, even if it is a single state, the use of the plural 'by some' (kehi ci) should be understood as being done because the number is not specifically limited.

## End of the Explanation of the Terms of Association and Dissociation in the Sixth Method.

## 7. Seventh Method: Explanation of the Terms of Dissociation from what is Associated

In the exposition of the terms of dissociation from what is associated (sampayuttena-vippayutta), the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha), etc., are not taken because they do not have association with those states. Although the truth of origin (samudayasacca), etc., have association with those states and dissociation from associated states, they are not taken because there is no dissociation from the aggregates, etc., which are dissociated from what is associated. Indeed, among the aggregates, etc., of other wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states that are dissociated from the consciousness-arisings accompanied by greed (lobhasahagata cittuppāda) which are associated with the truth of origin, there is no dissociation from any state. If it is asked, 'Are not those consciousness-arisings accompanied by greed themselves the four aggregates, one and a half bases, and one and a half elements? Therefore, should it not be said that there is dissociation from those states?' The answer is: No, because other states also have the nature of aggregates, etc. Those consciousness-arisings accompanied by greed alone are not the four aggregates; in fact, those states and other states besides them also constitute the four aggregates. Likewise, they also constitute the one and a half bases and elements. Other states do not become dissociated from those other groups, because the parts of a group and other groups that are parts do not have mutual dissociation. This method is the same for terms such as the truth of the path (maggasacca), the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya), and so on. Even in the case of states of 'sustained thought only' (avitakkavicāramatta), if initial thought (vitakka) is entirely desired, no reason is seen for not taking them, as they follow the same course as states with initial and sustained thought (savitakkasavicāra).

However, in the Commentary, the phrase 'states of such nature' (evarūpāni) means that just as the answer (vissajjana) is not appropriate for the aggregate of matter, so too for other terms where the answer is not appropriate, they are called 'states of such nature' due to the inappropriateness of the answer, and it should be understood that it is not because of the absence of association. By the words 'those terms which indicate states associated with the mind-object element (dhammadhātu)', the terms such as the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) are shown. By the words 'consciousness is also not mixed with other states', the terms such as the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) and the mind base (manāyatana), etc., are shown. There, 'not mixed with other states' means not mixed with dissociated states. Even the terms associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha vedanā) are taken here because they indicate consciousness mixed with associated states. By this characteristic, it is shown that only 'states of such nature' are taken; it does not show that 'states of such nature' are simply taken.
23:
This is because terms such as the truth of origin (samudayasacca) and the bases of power (iddhipāda) are not included (in this method). There is an ancient reading: 'Then the seven states of contact (phassasattaka) and consciousness, together with the associated terms, are seven.' However, considering this reading to be deficient, (ancient teachers) created the reading: 'Then the seven states of contact, three in the triads, and seven in the intermediate (mahantara) terms.' The words 'by means of those dissociated from the very term extracted for the question' are said considering that states dissociated from those associated with the term extracted for the purpose of the question are also dissociated from that term. In the summary verse (uddāna-gāthā) of the Pāḷi text, by the words 'and two associated with the mind, initial and sustained thought' (dve ca manena yuttā, vitakkavicāraṇā), the terms 'with initial thought' (savitakka) and 'with sustained thought' (savicāra) are shown, intending the two—initial thought and sustained thought—which are invariably associated with the mind element (manodhātu).

## End of the Explanation of the Terms of Dissociation from what is Associated in the Seventh Method.

## 8. Eighth Method: Explanation of the Terms of Association with what is Dissociated

In the exposition of the terms of association with what is dissociated (vippayuttena-sampayutta), because there is no state extracted in the Pāḷi text as being associated with what is dissociated from the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha), etc., it is not stated as: 'Those states which are dissociated from the aggregate of matter, with those states, which states are associated?' Instead, it is stated as: 'Those states which are dissociated from the aggregate of matter, with how many aggregates... (pe)... are they associated? There are none.' By this, it is shown that since those (four mental aggregates) dissociated from the aggregate of matter have no association with any aggregate, etc., the very state of 'associated with what is dissociated' as extracted does not exist; how then could there be association of that state again with aggregates, etc.?

## End of the Explanation of the Terms of Association with what is Dissociated in the Eighth Method.

## 9. Ninth Method: Explanation of the Terms of Association with what is Associated

In the explanation of the terms of association with what is associated (sampayuttena-sampayutta), the term 'by means of whichever aggregate, etc.' (yaṃkhandhādivasena) should be understood as a compound (samāsa); it means 'by the power of whichever state such as an aggregate'. The term 'of that very same' (tasseva) means 'of that very same aggregate, etc.' This is what is meant: In this ninth method, whatever associated state is mentioned, among the terms starting from the aggregate of matter and ending with the state without conflict (araṇa), it associates with whichever aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), etc.; then, having asked about the association of that very same aggregate of feeling, etc., with the aggregates, etc., the answer is given.
24:
The answer has been given. Because that dhamma, such as the aggregate of feeling, is associated with what is associated with itself, it is extracted as "associated with the associated." By this term "or by form" (rūpena vā), it should be understood that non-association with the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca), the unconditioned (appaccaya), and the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) is also stated. Similarly, by the term "or by those mixed with form" (rūpamissakehi vā), non-association with those mixed with Nibbāna, such as "neither acquired nor subject to clinging" (anupādinnānupādāniya), is also stated. For it will be said in the ninth method: "Nibbāna, however, has the same status as subtle form (sukhumarūpa)." The meaning of the term "by those comprising all immaterial aggregates" (sabbārūpakkhandhasaṅgāhakehi) is that since association can only be obtained with the mental aggregates that are present, it refers to association with terms such as the immaterial sphere (arūpabhava) which can comprise the four mental aggregates without deficiency, not excluding even a single dhamma among the mental aggregates that are currently arising.

The summary in this ninth method is: those dhammas such as the aggregate of form which do not obtain association are all not taken; all other dhammas such as the aggregate of feeling, other than the aggregate of form and so on, are indeed taken. This should be understood.

## The explanation of the Ninth Method: Associated with the Associated, is finished.

## 10. The Tenth Method: Dissociated with the Dissociated

In the exposition of the term "Dissociated with the Dissociated," among the dhammas not taken, dhammas such as the sphere of mental objects (dhammāyatana) are not taken because there is no dhamma dissociated from them, due to their being dhammas included in all consciousness-arisings (cittuppāda) mixed with Nibbāna and form without an object (anārammaṇa). Dhammas such as the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca), the four great existences, and the indeterminate (abyākata) are not taken because there is no dissociation from the aggregates and so on which are dissociated from those dhammas. This distinction should be understood.

## The explanation of the Tenth Method: Dissociated with the Dissociated, is finished.

## 11. The Eleventh Method: Associated and Dissociated with the Included

In the explanation of the eleventh method, these terms "And they, with the remaining three aggregates, with one mind-base, with the seven consciousness-elements" should be connected with the term "are called associated." To show the meaning of the term "with some" (kehici), by this Pāḷi "excluding craving (taṇhā) from the aggregate of mental formations, the sphere of mental objects, and the element of mental objects," it specifies the dhammas included by way of aggregates and so on in the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca) mentioned as "and they" (te ca); and of those very specified forty-nine mental formations excluding craving, with the remaining mental formations excluding themselves and craving, and with craving in the sphere of mental objects and the element of mental objects, and with the aggregates of feeling and perception...
25:
Regarding the state of being associated with those things worthy of association, it is said: "Because of being associated with the remaining things, they are called associated with some."

## The explanation of the terms 'included-associated-dissociated' (saṅgahitena-sampayutta-vippayutta) of the eleventh method (ekādasa-naya) is finished.

## 12. Explanation of the terms 'associated-included-excluded' (sampayuttena-saṅgahitāsaṅgahita) of the twelfth method

In the twelfth method, just as in the ninth method, only those things worthy of association are obtained; with this intention, it is said: "Only those very things are extracted."

## The explanation of the terms 'associated-included-excluded' of the twelfth method is finished.

## 13. Explanation of the terms 'excluded-associated-dissociated' (asaṅgahitena-sampayutta-vippayutta) of the thirteenth method

In the explanation of the thirteenth method, that which is not included by even the three kinds of inclusion is consciousness alone. The twenty-two things shown in the Pali text by the summary verse (uddāna-gāthā) beginning with "Rūpañca dhammāyatanañca" are called "things having problems similar to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha)". Those things which are not included by the three kinds of inclusion and are only gross bases (oḷārika-āyatana) like the formless existence (arūpa-bhava)—all such remaining things extracted in this method are called "things similar to the formless existence". "Remaining" refers to the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and so on mentioned in the fifth method; although they have the nature of not being inclusive (of consciousness etc.), they do not enter into the answer (vissajjanā) in this method, and thus are not extracted. Regarding things like the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) which are not even non-inclusive, there is nothing to be said. To show why the aggregate of feeling and so on do not enter into the answer, it is said: "By the aggregate of feeling...", etc. In that passage, "there is no association of those things" means that because of the mixture of material and immaterial things with those that are dissociated, there is no association. If those things were sometimes immaterial and material things not associated with all consciousness-elements, it is not that they lack dissociation; therefore, it is not said "there is also no dissociation". It should be understood that it is not because there is dissociation of things not included by the aggregate of feeling. Because of the absence of both association and dissociation, the aggregate of feeling and so on do not enter into the answer in this method. In this case, it might be thus: "By the aggregate of feeling, the seven consciousness-elements mixed with objectless things by way of aggregates etc. are not included; of those things..."
26:
"There is neither association nor dissociation," it is said. For all consciousness elements that occur with matter without objects (anārammaṇa), for the mental factors associated with all consciousness elements, and for both of these together—because they are not included by the three inclusions of aggregates such as the aggregate of feeling, aggregates such as the aggregate of consciousness, and bases such as the eye-base—the absence of both association and dissociation is the reason for not entering into the answer in this method. Dissociation is fourfold: dissociation by nature (jāti), dissociation by plane (bhūmi), dissociation by time (kāla), and dissociation by continuity (santāna). Among these four, "wholesome states, unwholesome states", etc., are dissociation by nature. "States of the sense sphere, states of the fine-material sphere", etc., are dissociation by plane. "Past states, future states", etc., are dissociation by time. "Internal states, external states", etc., are dissociation by continuity. Thus, dissociation should be understood in four ways.

## The explanation of the terms 'excluded-associated-dissociated' of the thirteenth method is finished.

## 14. The fourteenth method: The explanation of the terms 'dissociated-included-excluded' (vippayuttena-saṅgahitāsaṅgahita).

In the fourteenth method, it should be understood that terms such as the mind-object base (dhammāyatana) do not enter into the answer of dissociation because they are states occurring in all thought-arisings (cittuppāda) mixed with matter without objects and Nibbāna. Here, the three states such as birth (birth, aging, death) are merely the nature of ultimate realities (paramattha); therefore, in no way is there association or dissociation. Because internal and external states are the collection of all states, and because states such as 'untraceable and non-impinging' (anidassana-appaṭigha) are all thought-arisings mixed with matter without objects and Nibbāna, (there is no association or dissociation). In this fourteenth method, only the existence of inclusion and exclusion of states dissociated from states such as the truth of suffering is taken.

In the summary verse (uddāna-gāthā) of the Pali text, "samucchede na labbhanti" means they are not obtained in the final (fourteenth) method. "Mogha-pucchakena ca" means those states that are not obtained are not obtained because of the reason of the "empty question" (mogha-pucchā), meaning the question for those states has no answer. Alternatively, the "empty questioner" is the eighth method, and together with that eighth method, in the final method, these states are not obtained in any way because of the absence of even dissociation.

## The explanation of the terms 'dissociated-included-excluded' of the fourteenth method is finished.

## The Mūlaṭīkā of the Dhatukatha-pakaraṇa is completed.

## Puggalapaññatti-pakarana-mūlaṭīkā

## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa

## 1. Mātikāvaṇṇanā

In the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, the dhammas are collected by way of triads (tika) and dyads (duka). In the Vibhaṅga, they are analyzed by way of aggregates (khandha) and so forth. In the Dhātukathā, the distinctions such as inclusion (saṅgaha) and non-inclusion (asaṅgaha) of those collected and analyzed dhammas are taught. Following this, the Puggalapaññatti is undertaken to show the various designations (paññatti) by which those dhammas are made known, both according to their own nature (sabhāva) and by derivation (upādāya), starting with the words "Six designations" (cha paññattiyo).

Among those designations, the designation of "person, woman, man, deity, human," and so forth, which is made by grasping those dhammas that occur in a continuous sequence through the power of a non-substantial collection (asabhāvasamūha), is called the designation of persons (puggalapaññatti). The designation of other external matter (rūpa) and Nibbāna, through the power of their own substantial collection and their own specific nature, should be understood as the five types of substantial designation (sabhāvapaññatti), such as the designation of aggregates (khandhapaññatti). By that designation, all substantial designations analyzed in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and other books are included.

The designation of persons, however, is a non-substantial designation (asabhāvapannatti). Because it occurs by deriving from the natural dhammas such as those to be fully understood (pariññeyya) that exist within the continuity of beings, through various distinctions such as "one liberated in a certain time" (samayavimutta), all non-substantial designations such as the primary ones like "monastery" and "couch" are included.

To this extent, designation (paññatti) is twofold: designation of the existent (vijjamānapaññatti) and designation of the non-existent (avijjamānapaññatti). These two themselves, when mixed, become the other four designations. Therefore, it should be understood that by showing these designations, all designations are shown in this book. Among the six designations such as the designation of aggregates, this book is named "Puggalapaññatti" because it is based on the designation of persons, whose specific distinctions are not shown in other books but are shown only in this book. In the phrase "desiring to designate those dhammas in this book," the meaning is that it is desired to show them as the basis (vatthu) of designation. This is because in this book, one does not perform the act of designating, but rather shows the designations through their bases.
28:
## Khandhāti Paññāpanā
In the phrase "Aggregates are making known (paññāpanā)," all general and specific designations such as "aggregate" or "matter is earth" are called paññāpanā. It should be understood that this is said with reference to that meaning. In this term "paññāpanā," there are two meanings: showing (dassanā) and establishing (ṭhapanā); these are called illuminating (pakāsanā) and depositing (nikkhipanā).

Among those two, the act of making known by assigning names to various groups, such as "material aggregate... faculty of one who knows, one liberated in a certain time," saying "this has such a name, that has such a name," is indeed depositing (nikkhipanā). It is not a type of depositing like the physical arrangement of designated things like a couch in a location. The description of the agent, "Name-designation shows and also establishes," should be understood as being said with reference to name-designation being the cause for those various dhammas being shown and established, whether in the sense of state (bhāva) or instrument (karaṇa).

By the words "Vijjamānapaññatti" and so forth, the phrase "Pāḷimuttaka" (outside the Pāḷi) is used with reference to the six designations not yet included in the Pāḷi text. "Kusala-akusalasseva" means just like the manifestation of the wholesome and unwholesome. The meaning of the term "vijjamānassa" is "of the existent" (sato), and the meaning of that "sato" is "of that which has arisen" (sambhūtassa). Alternatively, "vijjamānassa sato" means being existent and thus arisen. Desiring to show that very meaning, he said "sambhūtassa." By that word, he rejects the state of non-existence.

Likewise, "avijjamānassa" (of the non-existent) means that it is not like the wholesome etc. which exist distinctly from the nature of the unwholesome etc., or like contact (phassa) etc. which exist distinctly from the nature of feeling (vedanā) etc. Rather, it refers to those five aggregates which, when grasped, give rise to the perception of "woman, man"; if those aggregates are removed, the nature of "woman" etc. as distinct from them does not exist in an ultimate sense, and thus it means "of the non-arisen" (asambhūtassa). Some teachers say the meaning is "that which does not exist in that manner (as aggregates) but exists in another manner (as designation)"; the judgment that should be said regarding that meaning has already been stated in the Paññatti-duka.

Although it does not exist as an ultimate reality (paramattha), because there is the act of grasping as "woman, man" with a mind free from wrong attachment while following worldly usage, it is called "established merely by worldly usage" (lokaniruttimattasiddhi). However, things like a "fifth truth" grasped with a mind accompanied by wrong attachment are neither established by ultimate reality nor by worldly convention; therefore, it is said "unobtainable in every way." In this Puggalapaññatti book, it is said with reference to the three types that appear in their own form: Vijjamānapaññatti, Avijjamānapaññatti, and Vijjamānena Avijjamānapaññatti.

The views of the teachers (ācariyavāda) should be applied without contradicting the method of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) already mentioned. Therefore, the phrase "It is called designation because of the sense of being designated" means it is called designation merely by the fact of being designated, because it does not exist as an ultimate reality. For even the designated meaning, being together with its own nature, obtains an ultimate name corresponding to that nature, and thus from other dhammas...
29:
(The conceptual name such as feeling, etc.) does not obtain a conceptual name that should be obtained from another phenomenon. A name that is not an ultimate reality (paramattha-sabhāva) does not obtain a name by its own nature because it lacks an ultimate nature. It obtains the name 'concept' (paññatti) only as a meaning designated by names such as 'being' (satta), etc. Meanings such as 'being', etc., also do not have an ultimate nature. This is because in meanings such as matter (rūpa) and feeling (vedanā), which exist with an ultimate nature, there is no nature that cannot be found either as identical to or distinct from matter, etc.

Kiriṭa means a crown; one who possesses that crown is called kiriṭī (one with a crown). In this teacher's tradition (ācariyavāda), since there must be complete characteristics, a comprehensive inclusion (into vijjamāna-paññatti, etc.) should be made. It is appropriate to say that concepts of comparison (upanidhā-paññatti) and concepts of juxtaposition (upanikkhittaka-paññatti) of types such as 'second', 'third', etc., fall into the six types of concepts (such as vijjamāna-paññatti) because they prioritize the countable meaning. The remaining concepts should also be included in their respective concepts as appropriate. Since numbers such as 'second', 'third', 'two', 'three', etc., do not exist at all in the ultimate sense, considering the status of those derivative concepts (upādā-paññatti) and continuity concepts (santati-paññatti) as concepts of the non-existent (avijjamāna-paññatti), and the status of other comparative concepts as concepts of the non-existent by means of the non-existent (avijjamānena-avijjamāna-paññatti), the author (of the Sangaha) says: "The remaining concepts belong to the side of the non-existent and the side of the non-existent by means of the non-existent." He considers concepts of comparison and juxtaposition such as 'second', 'third', 'two', 'three', etc., only as concepts of the non-existent by means of the non-existent. This is because those numbers designated by looking towards the first meaning or by placing them near the first meaning do not exist at all in the ultimate sense. Similarly, he considers the concept of continuity (santati-paññatti) only as a concept of the non-existent by means of the non-existent. Because neither the number eighty nor the person who is eighty years old exists in the ultimate sense.

The phrase "some concepts of planes" (bhūmi-paññatti) is said with reference to concepts such as the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), etc. The intention is that phenomena such as the sense sphere are ultimate realities. If the term 'kāma' is taken as the location (plane), this concept should be a concept of the existent by means of the non-existent (avijjamānena-vijjamāna-paññatti). If the aggregates produced by kamma are taken, it should be a concept of the existent by means of the existent (vijjamānena-vijjamāna-paññatti). Just as designating a person as a 'reciter' (bhāṇaka) due to the action called speech or the volition that produces speech falls into the category of a concept of the non-existent by means of the existent (vijjamānena-avijjamāna-paññatti), similarly, designating persons as 'lean' or 'stout' based on the shape called the visible-data base (rūpāyatana) should be a concept of the non-existent by means of the existent. Or, if shape is not taken within the visible-data base, it should be a concept of the non-existent by means of the non-existent. Concepts of the existent such as matter (rūpa) and contact (phassa) should be included in concepts of function (kicca-paññatti) by virtue of functions such as being deformed, etc., or in individual concepts (paccatta-paññatti) by virtue of the names of individual phenomena. Since the other four concepts formed by the combination of concepts of the existent and non-existent have already been mentioned, this teacher's tradition should be known as a comprehensive tradition.

Desiring to show the meaning of the Pali text "As far as the five aggregates" (yāvatā pañcakkhandhā), etc., the author states the passage "By as much designation" (yattakena paññāpanena), etc. In that passage, "As far as the five aggregates" means: by as much designation as the five aggregates exist, by that much is the concept of aggregates (khandha-paññatti) of the aggregates in brief. "As far as the aggregate of matter... the aggregate of consciousness" also means: by as much designation as the aggregate of matter, etc., exist, by that much is the concept of aggregates of the aggregates in detail. It should be understood that this meaning is stated by virtue of brevity and detail, having construed the Pali in this way. Indeed, the meaning of the Pali "The concept of aggregates of the aggregates" (khandhānaṃ khandha-paññatti) in "As far as the five aggregates" is shown by this statement: "Or, in brief, as the five aggregates by as much designation." However, the meaning of the Pali "As far as the aggregate of matter," etc., is shown by the statement "The aggregate of matter by way of detail," etc.

In that explanatory text, the words "aggregate of matter... aggregate of consciousness" are merely an indication of the divisions of the aggregates. Because of such indication, although not directly stated in the Pali, all divisions of the aggregates are included. Therefore, "Therein also, the aggregate of matter is of the sense sphere," etc., is stated. Alternatively, in showing this concept of aggregates, this is the construction of the meaning of the Pali: connecting the word "as far as" (yāvatā) with all words—as many as the five aggregates are, by that much is the concept of aggregates of the aggregates. As many as the divisions of the five aggregates are, and as many as the divisions such as the sense sphere of the aggregate of matter, etc., which are divisions of those five aggregates, by that much is the division of the designation of the concept of aggregates; thus he shows the division of the concept of aggregates by way of the division of objects stated in other texts. The same method applies to the words "As far as the bases" (yāvatā āyatanānaṃ), etc.

"By only a part" (ekadeseneva) means "only by way of brief indication" (uddesamatteneva).
