## 2. Niddesavaṇṇanā
## 1. Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā
With the intention that "Only the factors of absorption (jhāna) are liberations," [the commentator] said, "By the mental body (nāmakāya) associated with liberation." By the words "associated with which [mental body]," and so forth, he first explains the sense of endowment (samangībhāva). By the words "mental factors that are only touched by contact (phassa)," he explains the second sense, which is the sense of touching by contact (samphassa) as mentioned in "Moreover, this [contact]," and so forth; and by the remaining words, he explains the remaining senses of cause. Indeed, endowment, touching, and being a cause are called "touching" (phusanā). Furthermore, because the first sense (endowment) is difficult to understand, wishing to explain it, he said, "In that [jhāna], for that person," and so forth. Intending that the aggregates of feeling and the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) are included among the remaining fifty-odd states after excluding those [jhāna] factors, he said, "There are four aggregates."

In this case, since pleasure (sukha) should be touched by feeling and the faculty of joy, and since those three are not different (being of the same essence), does it not follow that it [feeling] touches itself? It does not, because it is stated that the nature of close contemplation (upanijjhāyana) is obtained through the sense of experiencing (vedayita) and the sense of predominance (adhipati). Alternatively, in the phrase "excluding those [jhāna] factors," the plural is used because there are many factors. Among those factors, each should be applied individually, such as "excluding initial thought (vitakka)," and so forth. In such application, in the case of "excluding pleasure (sukha)," the remaining aggregates are three; in other applications, they are four. In all applications, by including the three within the four, it is said, "There are four aggregates."

A person who has been liberated from some taints (āsavas) by non-temporary liberation (the Path) and is also endowed with the superior temporary liberation (jhāna) due to obtaining the support (upanissaya) for non-temporary liberation, that person alone is called "temporarily liberated" (samayavimutta). For such a person is a trainee (sekha) who has attained jhāna and is liberated from defilements by it, and since they do not return to the realm of form or the formless realm and are thus liberated from sensual lust and so forth, they deserve to receive the designation "temporarily liberated." However, a worldling (puthujjana) who has attained jhāna is of a nature to return [to the sensual realm], and because sensual lust and so forth can arise again, they are not called one liberated from defilements; therefore, they do not deserve the designation "temporarily liberated" and are not called "temporarily liberated." For an Arahant, there are no taints remaining to be liberated from, because they are already liberated. For that Arahant, the eight liberations (vimokkhas) are merely for dwelling happily in the present life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra). Therefore, the eight liberations of that Arahant are not the cause for the designation of being temporarily liberated or non-temporarily liberated. To show that they [the liberations] are not the cause, [the Buddha] said, "He does not dwell having entered the eight liberations," and so forth. This was not said merely to show the state of being non-temporarily liberated (asamayavimutta) only for the dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka). In truth, every Arahant is indeed non-temporarily liberated. In the statement "Every Arahant is indeed (non-temporarily liberated)," the dry-insight Arahant, the Arahant who has serenity as their vehicle (samathayānika), and the Arahant who attains the eight liberations are all included.
32:
## To show "Na heva kho... pe... viharati" was said; it should be understood that it was not said to show the state of being liberated at all times (asamaya-vimutta) only for the dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka). For every Arahant is one who is liberated at all times. "External" (bāhirānaṃ) means those existing outside of the supramundane (lokuttara); the meaning is "mundane" (lokiyānaṃ).

To show that the word "arūpa" does not merely signify the formless aggregates and Nibbāna, it is said: "Other than form (rūpa)" and so on. "Casket of the mind" (cittamañjūsaṃ) refers to concentration (samādhi). Because it is the basis for states such as the higher knowledges (abhiññā), concentration is like a casket. "To pervade the duration" (addhānaṃ pharituṃ) means to extend for a long time; the meaning is to continue. It should be understood that the breach of duty (vattabheda) occurs because of not being careful there after thinking "it should be swept."

However, an attainment lost merely by such a breach of duty is not like one lost through sensual desire (kāmacchanda) etc., which cannot be recovered by anything; because the obstacle is weak, it can be recovered merely by performing the duties and observances; thus it is said: "He sat down even while attaining."

Even for those who pass time with negligence appropriate to themselves, the attainment does not perish, so they are not called "fallen away" (parihīna); the intention is that they are capable of entering the attainment as soon as those various distractions are removed.

In the Sutta from the Saṃyutta Nikāya where it is asked: "Venerable Sir, why is it that gain, honor, and fame are an obstacle for a monk who is an Arahant?" the Buddha replied: "Ananda, for that Arahant, there is the unshakeable deliverance of mind (akuppā cetovimutti); I do not say that gain, honor, and fame are an obstacle to that deliverance of mind. But Ananda, those pleasant dwellings in this life (samāpatti) attained by that monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute—I say that gain, honor, and fame are an obstacle to those."

In that Sutta, it is said that gain, honor, and fame are an obstacle because the pleasant dwellings of attainment, which should be maintained by entering them from time to time, cannot be accomplished during the time of those various distractions. With this meaning, it should be understood that there is no contradiction between the Commentary and that Sutta.

In the passage "Dhammānaṃ... pe... pīti," it should be said "dhammehi." Here, because of the reason "he might fall away from those attainments," both the falling away and non-falling away of the person from the states of attainment are mentioned. There, because of the reason "those attainments might perish due to the person's negligence," both the perishing and non-perishing of the states are mentioned. Since the falling away of the person is indeed the destruction of the states of attainment, it should be understood that this is stated as another method (pariyāya) merely by the difference in phrasing or the difference in the literal meaning of the words.
33:
7-8. Volition (cetanā) refers to the volition of attainment (samāpatti-cetanā), which is the cause for the arising and entering of attainment, and the volition of striving (tadāyūhanā-cetanā), which is the cause for making an effort for that attainment. Protection (anurakkhaṇā) is mindfulness (sati) accompanied by wisdom (paññā) that can distinguish between factors beneficial and non-beneficial to the attainment. Because of being worthy of the attainments prompted and protected by that volition and protection, they are called cetanā-bhabba and anurakkhaṇā-bhabba.

Puthujjanagotta (the lineage of worldlings) refers to the training of worldlings, or the surpassing of the three trainings existing in the continuum of worldlings. These three trainings are called "training of worldlings" because they cannot absolutely cut off the three fetters (saṃyojana).

One who stands on the path of Arahantship (arahatta-maggattha) is also called bayūparata (one who desists through fear) because, being terrified of the danger of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-bhaya) through wisdom, he has desisted from the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana). Therefore, it is said, "The seven learners (sekha) are called bayūparata."

Those devoid of life-continuum wisdom (bhavaṅga-paññā) are taken as "those possessed of the obstruction of result" (vipākāvaraṇa). To show that even those with triple-rooted rebirth (tihetuka-paṭisandhi) are sometimes taken as "those of poor wisdom" (duppaññā), it is said, "those who have not yet obtained the strong support (upanissaya) for the path and fruit." This is because without wisdom, there can be no such support for the path and fruit.

Fixed states (niyata-dhamma) can only occur where there is a mixture of fixed and unfixed occurrences. To show that there is no "fixed individual" (niyata-puggala) in Uttarakuru because such a mixture does not exist there, it is said, "To the inhabitants of Uttarakuru..." and so on.

Among the thirteen heads (sīsa), the head of obstacles (palibodha-sīsa) and others, and the head of occurrence (pavatta-sīsa), are to be exhausted. The head of resolution (adhimokkha-sīsa) and others are the factors that cause exhaustion. The fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), which is the result of the path that causes exhaustion, is called the head of range (gocara-sīsa). This is because that fruit of Arahantship is the liberation of the fruit (phala-vimokkha), which is both the domain of the Buddhas and internal (ajjhatta). The head of formations (saṅkhāra-sīsa), which is the object of the path and fruit that cause exhaustion, is cessation (nirodha / Nibbāna), which is the seclusion from formations. To show the state of being "equal-headed" (samasīsī) by demonstrating the simultaneous completion of the factors to be exhausted and the object of the fruit that causes exhaustion, thirteen heads are mentioned in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. However, in this text, according to the words "the exhaustion of taints and the exhaustion of the life-faculty occur neither before nor after," the connection is made only by way of the heads of the occurrence of defilements, saying "Therein, the head of defilements (kilesa-sīsa)..." and so on. Therein, although the head of occurrence (pavatta-sīsa / life-faculty) is exhausted by the path that emerges from the round of rebirth by not allowing it to occur again after the death-consciousness, it continues to occur until the death-consciousness; therefore, "the head of occurrence..."
34:
"The life-faculty exhausts the death-consciousness," it is said. The stages of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-vāra) which are made to occur as if immediately after the exhaustion of defilements should also be called the stages of the exhaustion of defilements. According to the words, "When liberated, the knowledge occurs: 'It is liberated,'" the exhaustion of defilements is said to be completed by the conclusion of reviewing. If that conclusion occurs with the death-consciousness, then the conclusion of life also occurs with that same death-consciousness. Thus, because of the equality of the stage and the death-consciousness, the exhaustion of defilements and the exhaustion of life occur neither before nor after; this is expressed by the term vāra-samatāya (by the equality of the stage). In the phrase "entering the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), he attains parinibbāna," it should be understood that the parinibbāna death-consciousness itself is spoken of as "entering the life-continuum."

Mahāpayoga (great effort/action) is a great functional action (mahā-kiriya) that destroys destruction, similar to the manner of the arising of a great storm that causes destruction. "Tiṭṭheyya" means "destruction should not occur."

"Araṇīyattā" means "because of being worthy of being approached/cultivated."

The state of being a tevijjā (one with threefold knowledge) is primary (nippariyāya) when the supreme knowledge (agga-vijjā), which is the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), is attained, by which one's task is done. That state of being a tevijjā is also a superior tevijjā accomplished by way of the incoming knowledges (recollection of past lives and divine eye); thus it is said, "The incoming [knowledges] alone are the main [factors] (dhura)."

In the phrase "tattha ca," the locative case is used in the sense of cause (nimitta), or in the sense of the basis for the attainment of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). This is because one is said to have attained omniscience in that very [penetration of the Four Noble Truths].

"Ananussutesu dhammesu" means in the truths not heard before from others.

After teaching the eight liberations (vimokkha) ending with the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), starting with "One possessing form sees forms," it is said in the Mahānidāna Sutta: "Ānanda, when a bhikkhu dwells having touched these eight liberations with the mental body (nāma-kāya), and his taints are exhausted by his seeing with wisdom, this bhikkhu, Ānanda, is called 'liberated in both ways' (ubhatobhāgavimutta)." Although this was said, it was spoken by way of the most excellent 'liberated in both ways' person. In this Puggalapaññatti-aṭṭhakathā, however, for the purpose of including all 'liberated in both ways' persons according to the Kīṭāgiri Sutta, it is said, "He dwells having obtained the eight attainments with the co-nascent mental body."
35:
In the Kīṭāgiri Sutta, it is stated: "Here, monks, a certain person dwells having touched with the mental body those peaceful liberations that transcend forms, the immaterial attainments; and having seen the [Four Noble] Truths with the wisdom of the path of insight, his taints (āsavas) are destroyed. This person, monks, is called one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta)." Accordingly, four types of persons liberated in both ways have been taught by virtue of the four immaterial attainments. It should be noted that the supreme person liberated in both ways, who possesses the aforementioned characteristics, has also been taught. The same method applies to the body-witness (kāyasakkhī) person.

In the phrase "his taints are destroyed because of seeing with wisdom," it is not that the taints see with wisdom; rather, it is taught that the taints are destroyed because of the cause which is seeing. Since the destruction is dependent on seeing, seeing with wisdom is the preceding action.

The phrase "this person is one dependent on name (nāmanissitaka)" means that this person liberated in both ways, having been freed from form and while attaining immaterial attainments, is called "dependent on name" because of being freed again from those mental defilements from the state of depending on name. After citing the sutta that accomplishes the state of being liberated in both ways due to liberation from those two bodies, the intended meaning is: "He is called liberated in both ways because he is well-liberated from the two bodies." In the sutta, the Buddha declared the sage Upasīva, who attained the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), as "liberated in both ways" because he was liberated from the mental body (nāmakāya).

In the first tradition of the Elders, one is called "liberated in both ways" because of being liberated by two parts. In the second tradition, one is called "liberated in both ways" because of being liberated from two parts (the physical body and the mental body). In the third tradition, one is called "liberated in both ways" because of being liberated twice by two parts. This is the distinction between these three traditions. In these traditions, "liberated" should be understood as being liberated from defilements, or being liberated from the collection of the two bodies—the physical body and the mental body—through the suppression and eradication of defilements.

That the immaterial jhana is liberated from the mental body means it is liberated from the mental body known as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Because that immaterial jhana is liberated from the mental body by being remote from the hindrances, and from the physical body by the suppression of craving for form, it is called "liberated in both ways" in a partial sense. Therefore, the author of the Commentary intends that the immaterial jhana, which is the basis for the path of Arahantship, is suitable to be the cause for obtaining the name "liberated in both ways."

Regarding the statement that among these persons, not even one is an attainer of the eight liberations, even a single immaterial jhana of suppression, which is the cause of being liberated from the physical body and thus the cause of being liberated in both ways...
36:
...means not having attained the liberation. Even a person who has attained one of the immaterial jhanas is called "one who has attained the eight liberations" because they have acquired the cause for being liberated in both ways, and that immaterial jhana, being a part of the eight liberations, is capable of bestowing that name. Therefore, it is said, "But in the immaterial jhanas," and so forth.

In the phrase "phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikaroti," the end of the touched immaterial jhanas is called "phuṭṭhanta," meaning the time immediately following the touched immaterial jhanas. Here, the accusative case should be understood in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). It means one realizes through the means of realization throughout the time immediately following the touched immaterial jhanas. As in the passages such as "ekamantaṃ nisīdi," this term is an adverbial derivative (bhāvanapuṃsaka). A person who is liberated from the physical body and a part of the mental body by the liberation of suppression through immaterial jhana, for him, the liberation known as cessation (nirodha) is as if it were observed or revealed, but it has not yet been realized with the mental body. However, when some taints are exhausted by making Nibbāna the object, then it is realized by him. Therefore, because he realizes the realizable Nibbāna with the mental body as it was observed, he is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī); but he is not called "liberated" (vimutta) because some taints have not yet been destroyed.

By the phrase "diṭṭhattā patto," it shows the state of a person who has reached Nibbāna through vision (diṭṭhi), which is the knowledge of the path of Stream-entry that sees the Four Noble Truths. Alternatively, there is a reading "diṭṭhantaṃ patto," meaning he has reached it in the time immediately following the knowledge of the path of Stream-entry known as vision. From the fruit of Stream-entry up to the supreme path (of Arahantship), a person is called "one attained through vision" (diṭṭhippatta).

In the passage "rejecting this method as 'no'," the distinction in wisdom between the one attained through vision and the one liberated through faith (saddhāvimutta) is stated; however, the specific reason by which that distinction is reached is not stated. Seeing this fault of not providing a reason, it should be understood that the ancient commentators made the rejection. By the words "in the Agamas and Commentaries," it should be known that he confirms the conclusion regarding the diversity of the Agamas. By the passage "liberated while believing," it shows the state of being liberated by mere faith even though not yet liberated in every respect. Alternatively, "liberated through faith" (saddhāvimutta) means a person who is firmly resolved through faith.

"Paññaṃ vāheti" means he causes wisdom to proceed excessively. "Wisdom carries this person" means it causes him to go towards Nibbāna.
37: In this context, why is the word 'api' (even/also) used in the phrase 'even at the moment of the path'? If it is said that a person endowed with the Noble Eightfold Path exists only at the moment of the path, and only then is called a Sotāpanna, would that not be incorrect? It is not incorrect. Because the path gives the name 'Sota' (Stream) to the fruit (phala) consisting of eight or seven factors similar to itself, a person endowed with that fruit is also a Sotāpanna. Alternatively, because a person established in the fruit (phalaṭṭha) is indeed one endowed with the 'Stream' which is the non-declining path, the word 'api' is used. However, that person established in the fruit is not currently attaining the Stream as in the first moment of the path; therefore, because of having attained the Stream, it is appropriate to call them a 'Sotāpanna' from the first fruit onwards.  It is said: 'Monks, all those who have unwavering faith in me through wisdom are Sotāpannas. Among those Sotāpannas, five types of persons reach the end (attain Nibbāna) right here in this realm of desire (kāmabhava), and five types of persons reach the end after leaving this realm of desire.' Among such persons, since those starting from the second phalaṭṭha have distinct names, it is appropriate to call only the first phalaṭṭha person a 'Sotāpanna' to distinguish them from others; therefore, only that person is intended here. By the phrase 'understands through the path already attained,' it shows that the attained path is the strong dependence (upanissaya) for reflecting on the Four Noble Truths and so on. 'Sambodhiparāyaṇa' means one for whom enlightenment (the path that knows the Four Noble Truths) is the ultimate refuge. According to the second meaning, 'Sambodhiparāyaṇa' means one for whom enlightenment (the three higher paths) is the ultimate destination.  Since the word 'kula' (family) alone refers to a great family, it is said: 'the meaning is that they are born only in families of great wealth.'  'Khandhabīja' (seed of the aggregates) refers to rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhivijñāṇa). In the statement 'it is spoken of here only by way of reflection while staying in this realm,' it means that a Sotāpanna who possesses jhāna, even if they have not completely cut off the internal fetters (ajjhattasaṃyojana), is similar to an Anāgāmī (Non-returner) and has the nature of not returning; thus, they are not included in this counting (such as the Sattakkhattuparama). Only those who wander between the lower and upper desire realms, who are born in the desire realm, and who have inferior jhāna are intended to be counted here.  'The words that should be said' refers to words such as 'the state of being thinned out (tanubhāva) should be known through two causes.'  'Whether arisen or immediately after' means whether this person has arisen by way of rebirth, or immediately after arising, they produce the Noble Path. 'Whether not yet reached the middle of the lifespan' means before reaching the middle of that person's lifespan, within this interval...
38:
"He brings about the Noble Path" is the meaning of the Pali text here. In the Commentary, however, like the simile "the river before reaching the mountain," it means bringing it about before reaching the middle of the life-span. It should be understood that when used with the word "para," the word "hutvā" is used as a linguistic ellipsis because it follows the term "vemajjha" (middle).

"Upahacca" means having approached (the end of the life-span). By such approaching, it includes both exceeding the middle of the life-span and reaching the time near death. Therefore, it is said "having exceeded the middle," and so forth.

Because it carries one to the higher Brahma realms, it is called "Uddhaṃvāhī" (the stream of craving or the stream of saṃsāra). Because of that state of carrying upwards, it is called "uddhaṃvāhibhāvena." Although an "Uddhaṃsota" Anāgāmī in the Aviha realm does not attain Parinibbāna in that very realm, they go to one or another realm and attain Parinibbāna. Since that person has the states of "Asankhāra-parinibbāyī" and "Sasankhāra-parinibbāyī," ten types of Anāgāmīs are mentioned in the Aviha realm. The same method applies to Atappa and other realms. "Anupahaccatala" means not reaching the ground. The potential for speed or lack thereof in Asankhāra and Sasankhāra-parinibbāyīs should be understood as the difference between a spark that burns a small amount of grass and wood and a spark that burns a large amount. One should not assume superiority over an "Antarā-parinibbāyī" or "Upahacca-parinibbāyī" like a spark that goes out immediately after arising is superior, or lack of superiority like an ember that goes out only after reaching the ocean is not superior to an "Uddhaṃsota." This is because those Antarā-parinibbāyīs and others are themselves divided into two types: Asankhāra and Sasankhāra-parinibbāyī. The phrase "greater than that" is only intended to show a spark capable of burning grass and wood, not to show superiority or lack thereof in status.

"No cassa no ca me siyā" means if the five past causes such as ignorance (avijjā) and formations (sankhāra) did not exist, then these five present results such as consciousness (viññāṇa) would not exist for me. By saying this, it shows the occurrence of present suffering due to the causes of the past life, thus referring to the practice of observing the arising of the aggregates (udayadassana-paṭipatti) by way of the arising of causes. "Na bhavissati, na me bhavissati" means if the five causes do not exist in the present, the five results will not exist for me in the future. This shows the cessation of results due to the cessation of causes, thus it is the practice of observing the passing away of the aggregates (vayadassana-paṭipatti). Alternatively, all four sentences refer to the practice of observing emptiness (suññatā-paṭipatti) by prohibiting the self and what belongs to the self in the present and future.

"Yadatthi" refers to the five aggregates that exist. "Bhūta" refers to that which exists according to its ultimate reality (paramattha), seeing the nature of arising and passing away and emptiness, being merely mind and matter (nāmarūpa) devoid of the imagined states of woman, man, person, or being. It means that with a mind that recoils through the knowledge that repeatedly observes Nibbāna, which is free from the cycle, one abandons the five aggregates or the desire and lust (chandarāga) for those aggregates. It means one attains equanimity through insight (vipassanānupekkhā) and becomes one who looks on with equanimity through the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (sankhārupekkhā-ñāṇa). In the text "bhave na rajjati, sambhave na rajjati," some teachers say it means not being attached to both inferior and superior lives. In reality, the present life is called "bhava," and the birth to be obtained in the future is called "sambhava." Alternatively, the five aggregates that clearly exist in the ultimate sense are called "bhava," and the causal factor of attachment is called "sambhava." By not being attached to both, the practice of the trainees (sekha) is shown.
39:
"I abandon" means obtaining insight equanimity (vipassanā-upekkhā); it means one becomes equanimous through the knowledge of equanimity regarding formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa).

In the passage "not lusting after existence (bhava), not lusting after origin (sambhava)", some teachers say it means not lusting after either an ordinary (inferior) existence or a special (superior) existence. In fact, the present existence should be known as "bhava", and the existence acquired by taking up future birth (jāti) as "sambhava". Alternatively, "bhava" refers to the five aggregates which are manifest in the ultimate sense, and "sambhava" refers to the craving and lust (taṇhā-rāga) which is the cause of that existence. By not lusting after both bhava and sambhava, the practice of the trainees (sekkha) is shown. For, detachment from the five aggregates together with their cause, sambhava, is the practice of the trainees.

Thus, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, one sees this five-fold aggregate as it really is with right wisdom as being merely mentality and materiality existing in the ultimate sense. Having seen the five aggregates thus as they really are with right wisdom, one practices for the sake of revulsion, for the sake of dispassion, and for the sake of cessation regarding those five aggregates. Having seen the ignorance and craving which are the causes of those five aggregates as they really are, one practices for the sake of revulsion, for the sake of dispassion, and for the sake of cessation regarding that cause, sambhava. Having seen as it really is that whatever five aggregates have the nature of cessation due to the cessation of ignorance and craving—the causes of those five aggregates—one practices for the sake of revulsion, for the sake of dispassion, and for the sake of cessation regarding that thing which has the nature of cessation. Venerable Sir, one who practices thus is called a trainee (sekkha)."

"Then, further" means that such a person who does not lust correctly sees the higher peaceful state, Nibbāna, through path-wisdom (magga-paññā) by the sequence of insight. And that Nibbāna has not yet been fully realized in every respect by that Non-returner (anāgāmī), because that Nibbāna, which is to be realized only by the fourth path (arahatta-magga), has not yet been realized by him.

## The explanation of the Description of Ones (Ekaka-niddesa) is finished.

## 2. Description of Twos (Duka-niddesa)

Because some defilement (kilesa) has not yet been suppressed, the existence in the sense-sphere (kāma-bhava) which is not freed in some way is called "internal" (ajjhatta) because it is a special cause for grasping at a self (atta). In that internal state, the thing that binds is the "internal fetter" (ajjhatta-saṃyojana); a person associated with that internal fetter is called an "internal-fettered" (ajjhatta-saṃyojana) person.

One whose mind is associated with welfare, occurring without the cause of a favor previously done, is called "affectionate without cause" (akāraṇavacchala). Even if one expects a future benefit, if one acts based on that favor previously taken to heart, he is merely called "grateful" (kataññū), not "one who does a prior favor" (pubbakārī); this is the meaning of the statement beginning with "He will do for me". A person who is 'headed from darkness to light' (tamo-jotiparāyana) is called "one who does a prior favor" because he performs meritorious deeds without depending on the results of previous merit. It means that even if he does not perceive it as "I am paying a debt", he is as if he were doing so.
40:
Having obtained bear meat, one does not feel remorse thinking it is pork; this means that even while knowing it is bear meat, one does not feel remorse thinking it is pork, but rather overrides and violates the training rule.

"Titta" refers to a person (an Arahant) who has no further need for exertion because their task is completed.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Dyads is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Description of the Triads

"By the breaking of the remaining restraints" means either by the breaking of the restraint of the mind (manosaṃvara) or by the breaking of the restraint of mindfulness (satisaṃvara) and so forth. "By being endowed with unwholesome virtue" refers to being endowed with those things taught as: "Carpenter, what are unwholesome virtues? They are unwholesome bodily action, unwholesome verbal action, and evil livelihood (ājīva)." For him... "thus he has conduct accompanied by suspicion" means he has a manner of conduct that is suspicious.

To show the distinction among persons who have the same domain (visaya), it is taught starting with "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī) and so forth.

"Concentration is the beginning" means that the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) are, in the ultimate sense, called the Dispensation (sāsana). The foundational (pādaka) concentration, which has those supramundane states as its goal, is called the beginning of that Dispensation. Insight (vipassanā) is called the beginning because it is close to those supramundane states, and the Path (magga) is called the beginning because it is a part of the root of that Dispensation.

"A person with lap-like wisdom should be regarded as the lap itself" means that because of having wisdom like a lap, the person, like the wisdom, is like a lap. This is meant because the teachings (dhamma) do not remain long in that person. It will be said later, "It means one who has wisdom like a lap."

Just like the lap-like wisdom, the wisdom like an overturned pot should also be understood, because the teachings cannot enter and remain in that person.

Because it lasts for a long time and because it is firmly established, a person who has the inscription of anger arising from the offenses of others, which is like an inscription on a rock, is called "one who is like an inscription on a rock" (pāsāṇalekhūpama). The remaining persons should be understood in the same way.
41:
Pride that is empty and devoid of substance such as learning (suta) is called "naḷa" (reed) because it is like a reed. Because that person possesses an empty, boastful pride like a reed, he is called "unnaḷa" (haughty).

Regarding the phrase "Talk on virtue will also occur for us," it is said that "Talk on virtue does not occur at all" to show that the occurrence of talk on virtue, even as an initial effort, does not happen with an immoral person.

"In this or that" means that in various situations worthy of being supported, purified by wisdom, and developed, one is said to support with wisdom that has arisen based on superior virtue.

By the phrase "immorality like a cesspool," it shows only the similarity of immorality to excrement.

The phrase "They are unable to properly designate" refers to the fact that they are generally unable. Or, it refers to the inability of a person who, when the Tathāgata has appeared, tries to produce attainment (samāpatti) while being disrespectful toward Him. Or, it refers to the heretics (titthiyas) such as Pūraṇa Kassapa.

## End of the Explanation of the Triplets (Tika-niddesa-vaṇṇanā).

## 4. Explanation of the Quadruplets (Catukka-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

Immorality committed by others is done either through command or by one's own vocal effort (vacī-payoga). Therefore, one who inherits half of the evil caused by command is called "an heir to half of that."

By the word "this person," it refers to the method starting with "the first among them."

The accomplishment of the Dhamma taught in the discourse coming into the range of knowledge is called ñāṇugghāṭana (elucidation of knowledge). "Together with the time of being uttered" means precisely at that time, without it having passed, together with the time of being uttered.

By the word "that statement," it refers to the immediately preceding statement. When asked "What is the world?", the statement that stands encompassing a great meaning, "The five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) are the world," is a statement endowed with meaning (atthayutta). The statement "It is called the world because it disintegrates (lujjati)" is a statement endowed with reason (kāraṇayutta).
42:
"Sahitāsahitassa" means in speech connected with reason and speech not connected with reason. Or, it means in the determination by defining speech connected with reason and speech not connected with reason. "Only two" (dve yeva) refers only to the second and fourth persons. Because they are capable of making the Four Noble Truths known through the perfection of the teacher and the listener, they are called "natural Dhamma-preachers" (sabhāva-dhammakathika) (genuine Dhamma-preachers) or "preachers of the Truth-Dhamma" (sacca-dhammakathika).

The perfuming of the mind with wholesome states is called development (bhāvanā) or the burden of dwelling (vāsadhura). By the phrase "This person is a low person," the fourth person is meant, not the first. This is because the first person is intended to be like the Brahmin of Verañjā, who has no desire to deceive.

Similarity to the noble ones' going forward (abhikkamana) and so on in a person means that the person's going forward and so on are similar to the noble ones' going forward and so on. Or, it means having a similar going forward and so on because of the person's similarity to the noble ones' going forward and so on.

Calling an immoral person "immoral" is speaking of a fault that is evident. Instead of saying an immoral person due to killing is immoral due to stealing, saying he is immoral due to killing alone is speaking the truth about the fault. In the phrase "at the proper time," it is said that a certain person speaks at the proper time. To show what kind of person that is, the phrase "He is one who knows the proper time" and so on is said; thus, it is stated, "In that statement 'at the proper time,' which person..." and so on.

Āgamanavipatti (failure of arrival) is past kamma. Pubbuppannapaccayavipatti (failure of previously arisen conditions) is the parental semen and blood. Conditions that occur during the course of existence (pavatti) are pavatta-paccaya (conditions of occurrence), such as nutriment and so on. Because it illuminates, it is called joti (light). A person who shines through the perfection of family and so on is also called joti because he is like a light.

The reviewing of abandoned defilements and remaining defilements is also only the "knowledge and vision of liberation" (vimutti-ñāṇadassana) because it is the seeing of which defilements one is liberated from and which one is not. Thus, it is said, "Knowledge and vision of liberation is the nineteen-fold reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa)."

"Yāni kānici tantāvutānaṃ" means any of the cloths woven on a loom, without specification. Descending into the water in the evening is called sāyatatiya because it is the third time. Repeated application is called anuyoga. The word "anuyutta" (engaged in), as in "engaged in that application," should be understood as the second case ending (upayogavacana), or as a neuter abstract noun (bhāvanapuṃsaka) [adverbial].
43:
In that passage, "sikkhanabhāvena" means by way of practicing in the training (sikkhā), which is higher virtue (adhisīla), and in the code of discipline (sājīva), which is the Pāḷi text of the training rules. "Sikkhaṃ paripūrento" means fulfilling the restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara). "Sājīvañca avītikkamanto" means being one who does not transgress the words of the Blessed One, the training rules described as "the body of names (nāmakāya), the body of words (padakāya), the body of language (niruttikāya), and the body of syllables (byañjanakāya)." The combination of these two—fulfilling the restraint of virtue and not transgressing the code of discipline—is called "sikkhana" (training). Among these two, not transgressing the code of discipline is the cause for the fulfillment of the training in higher virtue. Indeed, it is said that by not transgressing the training rules of the code of discipline, the fulfillment of the restraint of virtue is achieved up to the Path (magga). "Vināsanabhāvato" means due to the nature of harming.

In the passage "haliddirāgo viya na thirakatho hoti," the similarity to cloth dyed with turmeric should be understood as the lack of firmness in speech, not in the person.

In the term "dārumāsako," the word "iti" indicates similar types of tokens (such as paper money, etc.). "Aññaṃ dassetvā aññassa parivattanaṃ" means showing a pair of cloths worth ten and giving a pair worth five while the buyer is unaware.

"Avikiṇṇasukha" refers to undistracted happiness through the power of perceiving beauty (subha), etc., in forms and so forth.

Insight (vipassanā) that proceeds by way of impermanence (anicca), etc., in the five aggregates is said to be "attained" only by the attainment of the Path and Fruit (magga-phala); because without that attainment, it does not remain stable. Therefore, only one who has attained the Path and Fruit is called "one who has attained insight into the Dhamma through higher wisdom" (adhipaññādhammavipassanālābhī). "Higher wisdom insight into the Dhamma" (adhipaññādhammavipassanā) should be understood as the knowledge of the Path and Fruit, both because it is wisdom superior to mundane wisdom and because it sees specifically into Nibbāna, which is the most excellent of all dhammas among the Four Noble Truths.

"Sutena anupapanno" means not being endowed with the Dhamma as heard or with the meaning such as virtue.

## The Commentary on the Description of the Fours (Catukkaniddesa-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Description of the Fives (Pañcakaniddesa-vaṇṇanā)

In the first group of five, the classification of persons can be known even by the summary (uddesa). Therefore, wishing to analyze those persons according to how one should practice towards them, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "tatra yvāyaṃ." "Ārambhasaddo" means the word that expresses the action of initiation (ārambhakiriya).
44:
With the arising of the Fruit of Arahantship, the task of the Path is completed; therefore, (the commentator) says, "Only the Fruit is spoken of by way of the task of the Path." "Āyācanasādhu" means 'sādhu' in the sense of a request, not in the sense of praise, etc.

"Ādheyya" is so called because it is placed in front in due order. "Mukha" should be understood as acceptance that proceeds like taking with the mouth by way of seeing, hearing, responding, and giving. A person who places such a "mouth" (acceptance) in front, or a person who places the natural mouth in front for the sake of acceptance, is called "ādheyyamukha." It means a person who places acceptance even in the first words spoken without investigation.

"Rajaggasmiṃ" means in the state of a mass of dust (rajaggabhāva).

The words "Milk is said to be the best from the cow" should not be connected in this way. Rather, having shown the five products of the cow (pañca gorasa) in their order of production, the words "gavā khīraṃ," etc., were spoken to show that among them, the cream of ghee (sappimaṇḍa) is the best. Therefore, (the commentator) says, "From the cow, there is what is called milk," and so forth.

## The Commentary on the Description of the Fives is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Description of the Sixes (Chakkaniddesa-vaṇṇanā)

In the description of the sixes, wishing to show that the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) and others, who are absolutely well-known, are persons with the qualities already mentioned, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "The Fully Enlightened One should be understood by that (quality)." In that Pāḷi, "tena" (by that) means by all these combined qualities: the self-realization of the Truths, the attainment of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) therein, and the attainment of mastery over the powers (bala). However, if it is said "by omniscience" (sabbaññutañāṇena), all this is included, because there is no omniscience without the self-realization of the Truths and the attainment of mastery over the powers. Therefore, in the Commentary, only "by omniscience" is stated. In that context, by the words "produced by oneself without a teacher," it negates the existence of a teacher for omniscience and its arising from another. It does not negate the omniscience produced by others who have teachers. This is because there is no such omniscience that ought to be negated.

## The Commentary on the Description of the Sixes is finished.

## 7. Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā

With the phrase "Faith is well-attained" (saddhā nāma sādhuladdhikā), by this Pali term "emerges" (ummujjati), it shows the wholesome state that emerges as "good," being faith that is included within wholesome states (kusala dhamma) or which is the predominant factor among the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya dhamma). The same applies to shame (hiri) and so forth. In this phrase "in wholesome states" (kusalesu dhammesu), the use of the locative case should be understood as indicating either inclusion within those wholesome states or as being of great benefit to those wholesome states. Also in this Sattakaniddesa, by the passage beginning with "Faith emerges well in wholesome states" (ummujjati sāhu saddhā kusalesu dhammesu), the arising of faith and so forth is shown through the wisdom that brings forth faith and so forth. For that very reason, it is said: "That faith of his does not remain" (tassa sā saddhā neva tiṭṭhati), and so on. Alternatively, by the passage "Faith is good in wholesome states," after stating the discourse showing the benefits that assist in emerging, by the word "emerges" (ummujjati), it should be understood that only the emergence known as faith is shown.

"In the filtering process" (caṅkavāre) refers to the cloth used by washermen for filtering lye. The continuity of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti) produced by a single kamma is called one thought-process (cittavāra). Therefore, referring to the second occurrence taken immediately after death, it is said "by the second thought-process" (dutiyacittavārena). The four types of persons, such as the one who stands after emerging, should be understood as many persons who do not realize the fruit of Arahantship in those respective births. However, the seventh person who realizes the fruit of Arahantship, although being a single individual, should be noted as becoming the seventh person at the end after having reached the state of the third person and so on in the preceding stage before becoming an Arahant.

## The Commentary on the Description of the Sevens is finished.

## 10. Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā

In the passage, "The ending for five persons in this life; the ending for five persons after leaving this life and ending in another life," those such as Stream-enterers (sotāpanna) who will attain Parinibbāna after being reborn in the fine-material (rūpa) or immaterial (arūpa) realms—even though they belong to the side of ending after leaving this life—are not included here in the context of rebirth in places common to worldlings (puthujjana) because they have not yet completely cut off the internal fetters (ajjhatta-saṃyojana). However, by virtue of rebirth in uncommon places (the Pure Abodes), only the five types of persons such as the one who attains Parinibbāna in the interval (antarā-parinibbāyī) are taught as "those who end after leaving this life and ending in another life."

## The Commentary on the Description of the Tens is finished.

## The Mūlaṭīkā on the Puggala-paññatti is completed.

## Kathāvatthupakaraṇa-Mūlaṭīkā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Explanation of the Introduction to the Text
By the phrase "kathānaṃ vatthubhāvato" (as the basis of the discourses), it is meant that this treatise, being a collection of discourses, serves as the locus for its own constituent parts (the individual discourses). Indeed, the parts are contained within the whole. To show the manner in which it was taught in brief, it is said: "established only by the setting down of the matrix (mātikā)."

## Explanation of the Narrative (Nidānakathā)
In the phrase "attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu)," the term Parinibbāna itself is expressed in the instrumental sense (as a cause) to distinguish it from the other Parinibbāna, which is the Nibbāna with residue (saupādisesa-nibbāna). Alternatively, it means that because that Nibbāna element was attained, the final consciousness arose without further rebirth; thus, that Nibbāna element is stated as the cause for the cessation of further rebirth.

Regarding the phrase "having a weak side," it is said to mean a king who rules only a single region (ekamaṇḍalika), rather than a powerful one like King Kālāśoka. However, it is also said to be "weak" because of the absence of wisdom capable of producing the distinction between those who speak according to the Dhamma (dhammavādī) and those who speak against the Dhamma (adhammavādī).

"Of those very persons" refers only to the members of the Bāhuliya sect; they are also known by the name Bahussutika. "The schismatics" (bhinnakā) refers to those who split from the original recital (Mūlasaṅgīti) or the original school (Mūlanikāya). The meaning is that they reached a state of dissimilarity in terms of views, suttas, and external marks or conduct.

"Mūlasaṅgaha" refers to the Council of the Five Hundred (Pañcasatika-saṅgīti). In phrases such as "collected elsewhere," it means that they extracted various suttas from the collection of suttas already compiled in the Dīgha Nikāya and others, and placed them elsewhere. Or it means they took suttas not included in the original compilation and placed them in some other Nikāya, or made them into something else. "The meaning and the text (attha and dhamma)" refers to the meaning of the Pali and the Pali text itself. "In the Vinaya and in the five Nikāyas" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka and the remaining five Nikāyas.
48:
The teaching starting with "Ānanda, I have taught feelings in two ways figuratively (pariyāyena)" (Majjhima Nikāya, Bahuvedanīya Sutta, etc.) is a discourse taught by way of figurative or indirect method (pariyāya). Indeed, the Blessed One's inclusion of neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) within peaceful and sublime pleasure (sukha) is the figurative method here. The teaching starting with "Monks, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neutral feeling" (Saṃyutta Nikāya, Samādhi Sutta, etc.) is a discourse taught by the direct or literal method (nippariyāya). Indeed, because the nature of feeling is threefold, this is the literal method.

The teaching starting with "Pleasant feeling is also impermanent and conditioned" (Dīgha Nikāya, Mahānidāna Sutta, etc.) is a sutta of explicit meaning (nītattha). The teaching starting with "Whatever is felt, all that is suffering" (Saṃyutta Nikāya, Kaḷāra Sutta, etc.) is a sutta whose meaning is to be inferred (neyyattha). (This is because pleasant and neutral feelings are 'suffering' only in the sense of suffering due to change, vipariṇāma-dukkha.)

In the teaching starting with "Monks, in three respects the people of Jambudīpa surpass the people of Uttarakuru and the Tāvatiṃsa devas" (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Tiṭhāna Sutta, etc.), the Blessed One spoke with reference to another kind of holy life (brahmacariya-vāsa, i.e., monkhood), but the [non-Dhamma speakers] took it and established a different meaning. They also took the sutta starting with "There is no living of the holy life among the devas" and, though it was spoken with reference to one meaning, they established it as having another meaning; thus should the meaning be understood here. By the shadow of the words (literal phrasing) such as "A certain person practices for his own benefit," they destroyed many subtle meanings such as emptiness (suññata/anatta).

"Vinayagambhīra" (profound Vinaya) means discarding a profound portion of the Vinaya (such as the Mahāpadesa or Parivāra). Or it means discarding a sutta that is profound because it can dispel defilements. "Patirūpa" (counterfeit) refers to a sutta that conforms to one's own desires, or a non-sutta that resembles a sutta. Some discarded only the Aṭṭhakathā-kaṇḍa (of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī), while others discarded the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Therefore, it is said (in the Dīpavaṃsa), "Discarding the six books of the Abhidhamma." Although the Kathāvatthu is subject to dispute (vivāda), the other six undisputed books of the Abhidhamma should be recited. To show that those six books no longer existed in the mouths of the non-Dhamma speakers, it is said "six books." Or, it is said "six books" by virtue of the six Abhidhamma treatises that were well-known even before the Third Council.

"Other" refers to other Abhidhamma treatises and so on. "Name" (nāma) refers to the names of Nikāyas that are not associated with the Buddha and others, such as Mañjusirī. "Mark" (liṅga) refers to the specific shape or form created by specific ways of dressing and cloaking. "Requisites" (parikkhāra) refers to items like the carrying-loop (sikkā). "Deportment" (ākappa) should be understood as the specific way of positioning the limbs during standing and so on. "Activity" (karaṇa) refers to specific tasks like sewing robes.

Because they split from the sect or doctrine called Kassapika, they are called "Saṅkantika." Those who split in succession from the Saṅkantika doctrine are the "Suttavāda" individuals. "Bhinnavāda" (schismatic doctrine) is so called because there are divergent doctrines within this [Theravāda context]. When counted together with that [original Theravāda], they become the eighteen doctrines.
49:
The meaning is that together with the undivided Theravāda, there are eighteen doctrines. Alternatively, "bhinnavādena" means there are eighteen by way of divergent views; all those together make eighteen. In the term "Theravādānamuttamo," the word "Thera" is an uninflected designation. That which belongs to the Elders (Theras) such as the Venerable Mahākassapa is "Thera." What is that? It is the doctrine (vāda). The meaning here is that the doctrine of the Elders is the best among doctrines.

With reference to doctrines that have already arisen, it was said: "the crushing of the doctrines of others (parappavāda-mathana)." Because it has the characteristic of preventing doctrines that will arise in the future, it is called "a sign for the future (āyatilakkhaṇa)."

## The Explanation of the Narrative (Nidānakathā) is finished.

## Mahāvaggo
## 1. Puggalakathā
## 1. Suddhasaccikaṭṭho
## 1. Anulomapaccayannīkavaṇṇanā
Things like pieces of brick that are seen in the form of gems due to magic are called 'māyā' (illusion). Objects such as magical creations and mirages, which are perceived by the mind in the form of unreal gems or water, are not 'saccikaṭṭha' (real in the true sense) because they possess an unreal nature of being known. To show that a sense such as form or feeling, which is not like those magical creations or mirages but exists truly, is called 'saccikaṭṭha', the Buddha said: 'Māyā ... bhūtattho' (Illusion ... the real sense). A sense perceived through hearsay and so on may be as heard or may be otherwise. Therefore, such a known sense is not 'paramattha' (ultimate reality); only the sense personally realized by oneself is 'paramattha'. To show this, he said: 'Anussavā ... uttamattho' (Hearsay ... the highest sense).

In the word 'chalavādassa', it means the speech that expresses a sense common to the dhammas such as form, which are stated as 'exists' (atthi) by the commonality of the word 'exists'. However, because of the statement 'That person admits ... saccikaṭṭha', it cannot be called 'chalavādassa' (deceptive speech). This is because the view is not 'chala' (deception). 'Okāsaṃ adadamāno' means desiring to cut off the basis [of the argument]. The meaning is: if a person could be obtained by way of 'saccikaṭṭha' (real sense), they should be obtainable like form and so on; since they are not so obtainable, your doctrine cannot stand—thus he refutes it. By the phrase 'taṃ sandhāya', he shows that he refers to the various dhammas mentioned in the Pali passages such as 'rūpañca upalabbhati' (and form is obtained), which are shown by way of being 'sappaccaya' (conditioned) and so on, as stated in 'yo saccikaṭṭho'.

After saying 'tena saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena', the intention of the commentator in saying 'tenākārena' is that a nature obtained by way of the mode of 'saccikaṭṭhaparamattha' is said to be obtained by 'saccikaṭṭhaparamattha'. If it were otherwise (if the mode and the possessor of the mode were different), instead of 'tato', it should have been said 'by that mode of that dhamma'. What is the difference between this second question and the first question? In the first question, it is meant: just as the fifty-seven various dhammas are obtainable by their true individual nature (sabhāva), is the person also obtainable? In this second question, however, it asks: those various dhammas which are obtainable by their true individual nature, are they obtainable by the mode of changeability (ruppana) or being conditioned (sappaccaya) and so on? By that mode...
51:
...is the person also obtained? This is the difference. Just as feeling, which is obtained by its true individual nature like form, is not obtained by the mode of changeability (ruppana), so too the person, who is obtained by true individual nature like the fifty-seven various dhammas, is not obtained by the modes of changeability or being conditioned and so on—this could be argued by the opponent (paravādī), and thus this point would not be open to challenge. Since the opponent's rejection would be appropriate, censure (niggaha) should not be applied. However, because no other real sense (saccikaṭṭha) exists apart from the fifty-seven various dhammas, the challenge is made only by way of the modes of those fifty-seven dhammas. By that very rejection, the fault that leads to censure is shown. The groups of admission and rejection are distinguished as the side of admission, the side of rejection, the affirmative side (anuloma), the negative side (patiloma), the first method, and the second method, due to commonality (sāmaṇya) and specificity (visesa). This should be understood as the difference between these methods.

The proponent (sakavādī), saying 'Tena vata re vattabbe', should be understood as saying 'because it leads to censure' with the intention that the opponent incurs a fault by not saying what ought to be said. It has been said: 'Thus, because the four applications (pāpanā) and impositions (ropanā) are stated by way of censure and the affirmative and negative, it is called the Fivefold Affirmative (anulomapañcaka) starting with "upalabbhati".' However, by way of the affirmative and negative, there should be seven (sattaka) including the two placements (thapanā). Otherwise, the reason for excluding those two placements should be stated. With the intention of saying later: 'A placement (thapanā) is merely the setting up of the opponent's side to show "this is your fault"; it is not a part that can clearly demonstrate censure (niggaha) or rebuttal (paṭikamma),' the two placements are excluded here as well. Just as the fourfold rebuttal (paṭikammacatukka) will be mentioned there instead of the fivefold rebuttal, here too the fourfold censure (niggahacatukka) should be mentioned. However, in a pure censure (suddhikaniggaha) where rebuttal is not mixed, since censure is primary, it should be understood that censure alone is mentioned separately as a summary. In the view of the teachers who say 'Because it is not a true censure, rebuttal is not mentioned separately there,' in the second opening of the discourse (vādamukha), it would result in the fourfold censure and the fivefold rebuttal.

The 'saccikaṭṭha' intended by oneself refers to conventional truth (sammutisacca). For it will be said: 'Referring to pure conventional truth or conventional truth mixed with ultimate reality, the opponent asks again: "yo saccikaṭṭho".' In that case, if the 'saccikaṭṭha' intended by the opponent is conventional truth, then the opponent, who has the same view as the proponent saying 'the person is obtained by way of conventional truth,' should not be refuted. The meaning is this: the opponent (*paravādī*), intending the *saccikaṭṭha* which is conventional truth (*sammuti-sacca*) as desired by him, says "There is that which is *saccikaṭṭha*," and so on. The fault might arise that the proponent (*sakavādī*) also desires only conventional truth as *saccikaṭṭha*. If both he and the proponent desire both conventional truth and ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*) as *saccikaṭṭha*, then it should not be said again, "He says this by combining conventional truth and ultimate truth."

If both truths are *saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*, the proponent who desires the apprehension of the person by a part of *saccikaṭṭha* (i.e., conventional truth) should not conduct an inquiry such as "Is the person apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact?" nor is an inquiry by a part of *saccikaṭṭha* appropriate. For it is like not being appropriate to inquire whether feeling (*vedanā*), which is apprehended by the mode of being felt (*vedayita*), is apprehended by the mode of being deformed (*ruppana*). The opponent also does not desire the person as having the nature of being deformed, etc., but rather desires the person only as *saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*. If there exists a *saccikaṭṭha* called conventional truth other than ultimate truth, the ultimate truth-ness of that person who is conventional truth should not be inquired into. In the view of teachers who say that the opponent asks intending that conventional *saccikaṭṭha* by attributing the term *saccikaṭṭha* to a person who is not *saccikaṭṭha*, the status of that conventional *saccikaṭṭha* as the *saccikaṭṭha* desired by him is not appropriate. Regarding the status of both conventional *saccikaṭṭha* and ultimate *saccikaṭṭha* as *saccikaṭṭha*, the fault is just as previously stated.

The meaning of *saccikaṭṭha* apprehended by the mode of conventional truth might be apprehended by the mode of true nature (*bhūta-sabhāva*), or it might not. If it is apprehended by the mode of true nature, the opponent who admits "The person is also apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact" should not be inquired into. If it is not apprehended by the mode of true nature, the *saccikaṭṭha-paramattha* mode of the person who is conventional truth, being free from that true nature, should not be stated, because it is not established. It will be said later: "Just as form (*rūpa*) and so on exist by way of individual characteristics (*paccatta-lakkhaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*), the person does not exist in this way." Therefore, the intention of the commentator should be sought here.

In the phrase "of the two truths" (*dvinnaṃ saccānaṃ*), since it is not apprehendable by the mode of the combination of the two truths, this non-attainment should be allowed; otherwise, nothing at all should be said. For just as non-attainment by a part which is the ultimate mode is not a reason for allowance, so also attainment by a part which is the conventional mode is not a reason for rejection; the intention of the commentator should be sought here as well. In the phrase "the mere generality of the word 'is not apprehended'" (*nupalabbhatīti vacanasāmaññamattaṃ*), it means that based on this sophistry (*chala-vāda*), this very word "is it not apprehended?" is both allowed and rejected. Just as I should be refuted by the allowance and rejection of this very word "is apprehended," so also you should be refuted by the allowance and rejection of this very word "is not apprehended." Thus, although it is similar to a statement that should be a ground for refutation (*nigga-haṭṭhāna*), treating a statement that should not be a ground for refutation as one is what constitutes sophistry (*chala-vāda*) here. Therefore, the mere general word "is not apprehended" is called "sophistry" because it is the cause of sophistry. And the mere general word...

7-10. After saying "The opponent's admission is based on his own view," it was said again, "The opponent's rejection is because the person does not exist in the ultimate sense." ## 7. Explanation of the Comparison of the Fourfold Method

46-52. An opponent who does not wish for the person to be different from even a single phenomenon among the fifty-seven types of phenomena should not be questioned or examined by way of each individual phenomenon such as form (rūpa). The reason is that, to prevent the opportunity for this opponent—who does not wish for the person to be different from the collective whole of phenomena like form and feeling, but rejects non-difference from a part such as form—to say that they do not deserve refutation, the [Commentator] said "And this inquiry" (ayañca anuyogo), etc. "Sakalā" (the whole) means intending the entirety in this way: "Are the fifty-seven types of phenomena the person?" or "Is the ultimate truth the person?" Having thus considered the entire ultimate reality, because the characteristic of inquiry and examination is established by way of the sequence of the Pāḷi text, and because there is no person in the sense of ultimate reality (saccikaṭṭha) other than the entire ultimate reality, it is meant that it is appropriate to impose a refutation on the opponent who rejects the question "Is form the person?" on the grounds that a person who is an ultimate reality cannot be other than that entire ultimate reality.

"Sabhāgavinibbhogato" means by way of having a nature such as feeling, etc., which is different from the nature of form. By the words "all phenomena" (sabbadhammā), it refers to all the remaining fifty-six phenomena, excluding form. In the context of "the person exists in form," the [Commentator] said "due to the fear of annihilationist view" (ucchedadiṭṭhibhayena ceva), with the intention that the opponent rejects it out of fear that if form, which is the support, is destroyed, the person will also meet with destruction. However, in the three [inquiries], the rejection is intended because of contradiction with their own doctrine. It is appropriate to say that although that opponent does not desire identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), they reject it out of fear that eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi) might arise. For among the twenty types of identity view, five are annihilationist views and the remaining fifteen are eternalist views. In the phrase "other than form" (aññatra rūpā), it should be understood that the meaning "the person who possesses form" is also included.

## 13. Explanation of the Inquiry into Human Action

"Mere instrument" (karaṇamatta) refers to the aggregates (khandhas) that exist in the capacity of being the producers of actions or the instigators of others.

Intending that there is no birth of a person apart from past kamma, nor is there the occurrence of right or wrong in the livelihood, arts, etc., of a person who has been born, he said "Past kamma alone is his" (purimakammameva tassa), etc.

Regarding the term "of the round of kamma" (kammavaṭṭassa), they say that there is no cutting off of the round of kamma in this way: "He who is the doer of the doer of kamma must also perform another kamma; the doer of that [doer] must also perform another." It should be investigated whether the doer of the person becomes the doer of kamma. It should also be investigated that for one who desires a doer of that person—such as the cause being the parents—a succession of doers (kārakaparamparā) of the performers of kamma arises.

"Due to the fear of contradicting the Suttas" (suttavirodhabhayena) means due to the fear of contradicting such Suttas as: "Brahmin, [to think] 'He who acts is the same one who experiences [the result]' is one extreme."

The meaning is that because of the teaching "He rejoices here, he rejoices hereafter," one acknowledges that it is the same person at the time of performing kamma and at the time of experiencing the resultant fruit (vipāka).
61:
When asked whether pleasure and pain are self-made, the Buddha rejects it because it contradicts the Sutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya which states: "O Kassapa, it is not so," in response to the question, "O Venerable Gotama, are pleasure and pain self-made?"

"This is merely a view" means that the same single person is neither the one who acts nor the one who feels, nor is he another; therefore, such a meaning does not exist. Thus, for one who speaks in this way, the fault of "not being self-made" and so forth follows; this is the intention. Furthermore, by the word "api ca" and so forth, this meaning is shown: it does not mean an inquiry such as "he acts" according to the will of another. Rather, among the views such as "he acts," when one does not desire one view, another view arrives. If that other view is also not desired, yet another view arrives. Thus, standing in the desire of the doer and the feeler, among the views such as "he acts," the inquiry is made by the power of the fault that arises from not accepting each particular view. Alternatively, it is shown that this inquiry is made not only because all faults such as "he acts" arrive, but also because each individual fault arrives. By the words "only in the previous manner," it is shown that all reasons for confession, such as "he rejoices in this world," should be combined and compared together.

## 14. Abhiññānuyogavaṇṇanā

In the phrase "achieving Arahantship by means of the inquiry into higher knowledge and so forth," the meaning included by the word "ādi" (and so forth) should be understood as the inquiry into higher knowledge: "Is there anyone who can perform a miracle?", the *ṭhapanā* (proposition): "If there were someone who could perform a miracle," and the *pāpanā* (consequent fault): "If it were so, then..." and so forth. Here, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) is called higher knowledge (abhiññā). The achievement of the Arahant who possesses that higher knowledge is called "arahattasādhanā." ## 19. Paṭivedhānuyogādivaṇṇanā
By the word "pariggahitavedano" (one who has comprehended feelings), it is shown that the knowing of one who has not comprehended feelings, thinking "I am happy, I am sad," is not called "knowing with wisdom" (pajānana), and it also shows the ability of the practitioner (yogāvacara) to distinguish even subtle feelings.

"Lakkhaṇavacanaṃ" (the word on characteristics) means that occurring within the form is being with form (saharuūpabhāva), and departing outside the form is being without form (vinārūpabhāva).

"Imā kho" (these indeed) means that the gross acquisition of self, the mind-made acquisition of self, and the formless acquisition of self are merely the world's designations (sammaññā). The Tathāgata speaks using these names without misapprehending them. Whether it be true or empty, although that self is not found, precisely because it is not found, he does not give rise to the wrong view of self (attadiṭṭhi) through misapprehension, but speaks only by the power of the conventional usage of "acquisition of self" (attapaṭilābha) that exists in the world; this is the meaning here.

In this context, by rejecting the existence of a person through the power of individual characteristics (paccattalakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa), and saying that it exists by worldly convention, it is meant that "there is no such nature as a person." For if that person existed by his own nature, he should be said to exist by nature, not by worldly convention. ## 2. Discussion on Falling Away (Parihānikathā)

## 1. Commentary on the Discussion of Falling Away in Terms of Argumentative Logic

"Bhikkhus, these two things lead to the falling away of a trainee bhikkhu" (A. Ni. 2.185). This sutta is not a basis for the view that an Arahant falls away; rather, it is a basis for the view that those such as Non-returners (Anāgāmīs) fall away. Therefore, in the statement "They also desire the falling away of an Arahant," the word "also (pi)" should be construed as "they also desire the falling away of a Non-returner and a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī)."

"In the third point as well, only those with dull faculties (mudindriya) are intended; the view that there is no falling away for all of them is his view"—this is the old version. However, if only those with dull faculties were intended, then a rejection (parikkhepa) should not have been made, but now a rejection has been made. Therefore, later teachers read it as: "In the third point as well, only those with sharp faculties (tikkhindriya) are intended; the view that there is no falling away for all of them is his view."

"Taking the meaning improperly" means that because only the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) is called "one who is fixed (niyata)," one takes the meaning that only that Stream-enterer does not fall away, while others do. Alternatively, some say it means taking the meaning "he is fixed in the sense of not falling away from the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala)," without taking the intended meaning of "he is fixed for the sake of the higher paths."

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Falling Away in Terms of Argumentative Logic is finished.

## 2. Commentary on Falling Away by Comparing Noble Persons

In the passage beginning with "In this case, he who...," one should examine the statement that the opponent (paravādī)—who desires the attainment of Arahantship immediately after one stands in the fruit of stream-entry, and the falling away from that Arahantship to stand again in that fruit of stream-entry—does not desire the attainment of Arahantship immediately after that fruit of stream-entry through renewed effort.

By the phrase "one who has attained jhāna but not yet reached mastery (vasībhāva)," it should be understood that a trainee (sekha) is meant. As for a worldling (puthujjana), whether he has reached mastery or not, he is not included in the text (tanti) concerning the temporarily liberated (samaya-vimutta) and the non-temporarily liberated (asamaya-vimutta). However, it is said that if he is included, he may be considered temporarily liberated by virtue of the defilements suppressed by meditative attainment (samāpatti).

## The Commentary on Falling Away by Comparing Noble Persons is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Discourse on Abandoning (Jahati)
## 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Not Citing Suttas (Nasuttāharaṇa)
"Kiccasabbhāvaṃ" refers to the state of having abandoned the internal fetters (saṃyojana) that are to be abandoned by the three lower paths. The view that this act of abandoning is completed by that very path of the Non-returner (anāgāmimagga) and the view that sensual lust (kāmarāga) and ill-will (byāpāda) are already abandoned during the state of a worldling (puthujjana) do not agree. Therefore, the meaning is that even though sensual lust and ill-will were abandoned (by suppression/vikkhambhana-pahāna) during the worldling stage, when the path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) arises, they can never arise again; thus, the function of abandoning by the three paths is appropriate.
