## 5. The Discourse "Everything Exists" (Sabbatthi)
## 1. Commentary on the Logic of the Argument (Vādayutti)
"Sabbasmiṃ sarīre sabbaṃ" means: are there feet in the head, or eyes in the back, etc.? Does everything exist in the whole body? "Sabbasmiṃ kāle" means: does youth exist in childhood, or childhood in old age, etc.? Does everything exist at all times? "Sabbena ākārena" means: does yellow exist in the mode of blue, or red in the mode of yellow, etc.? Does everything exist in every mode? "Sabbesu dhammesu" means: is there the ear in the eye, or the nose in the ear, etc.? Does everything exist in all phenomena?

By the word "ayuttaṃ," it means devoid of union (conjunction). However, that phenomenon has a single nature (ekasabhāva). To show the question "How can a phenomenon with a single nature be devoid of union?", it says "Nānāsabhāvānañhi," etc. Only two fingers or two rams, which have different natures, can have mutual union; there can be no mutual union in a single thing. Therefore, a single nature that is devoid of the union occurring between things of different natures is called "ayoga." In the Pali "Idaṃ pucchati," it means: taking the opponent's view as wrong view, when it arises, he asks "Is my own view right view (sammādiṭṭhi)?"
68:
Taking the opponent's view as wrong view, when it arises, he asks whether his own view exists as right view.

## The Commentary on the Logic of the Argument is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Comparison of Times (Kālasaṃsandana)

In the phrase "Having abandoned the past and future, making only the present matter unlovable and indivisible" (Atītānāgataṃ pahāya paccuppannarūpameva appiyaṃ avibhajitabbaṃ karitvā), it means that by both the words "present" (paccuppanna) and "matter" (rūpa), only present matter is spoken of. By the phrase "Because the designation has not departed" (Paññattiyā avigatattā), this meaning should be understood: Just as the designation "matter" (rūpa-paññatti) is a real designation (vijjamāna-paññatti) occurring in the sense defined by the nature of being molested (ruppana), the designation "cloth" (vattha-paññatti) is not a real designation occurring in a sense defined by nature. In truth, it is only an unreal designation (avijjamāna-paññatti) based on a collection of matter (a collection of threads) occurring in a sequence of before and after. Therefore, in the case of cloth, if the white color disappears, it is appropriate to say it is not [white]. However, in the case of matter, if the present state disappears, it is inappropriate to say it is not [matter].

## The Commentary on the Comparison of Times is finished.

## Commentary on the Clarification of Terms (Vacanasodhana)

In the phrase "Having been future or present, it is" (Anāgataṃ vā paccuppannaṃ vā hutvā hoti), it should be noted that when a future phenomenon becomes future and then becomes present, it is said to be "having been future, it is present." Similarly, when a present phenomenon becomes present, having previously been future, it is now present; thus it is said "having been, it is." "Does that also exist for you, having been?" (Kiṃ te tampi hutvā hoti) means: because of the non-departure of that state of "having been, it is," it is a question about the non-cessation or continuity of the state of "having been, it is." "Because there is no further 'having been' for what has already been" (Hutvā bhūtassa puna hutvā abhāvato) means: because a phenomenon that was future and has become present does not become future and present again.

Since that phenomenon which was future and became present is reckoned as "having been, it is," therefore, the teacher's intention is that he admits the second expression "having been, it is" is also appropriate. To one who speaks of the non-cessation of the state of "having been, it is" regarding ultimate phenomena (dhamma), the non-cessation of the state of "not having been, it is not" regarding non-ultimate things like a rabbit's horn (sasa-visāṇa) would follow; with this intention, it says "Atha naṃ," etc.
69:
"Paṭikkhittanayenāti" means by way of the distinction of time. "Paṭiññātanayenāti" means by way of the non-distinction of meaning. Even if one desires the non-distinction of meaning, it should be examined how one can admit the state of "hoti" (is/becomes) spoken of in the present for a future thing, and the state of "hutvā" (having been) spoken of in the future for a present thing. This is because that person only allows the non-distinction of meaning, but does not allow the state of the present in the future, or the state of the future in the present.

"Having changed the previously rejected question" means that since a fault has already been stated in the words "hutvā hoti, hutvā hoti" of the admitted question, one bypasses that stated fault and takes up the rejected question again to challenge with those words. In this context, if it is asked how there is a fault for one who admits "hutvā hoti" through the non-distinction of meaning because of the rejection of the question "Is the future the present?" due to the distinction of time, the meaning is that it is because that person admits the first question but rejects the second.

"Each one" means that it is not that the future thing alone is "na hutvā na hoti" (not having been, it is not), nor is the present thing alone; taking both, it is said "each one is na hutvā na hoti, na hutvā na hoti." It is not said that only each one is na hutvā na hoti, na hutvā na hoti. This method is the same for the previously stated words "each one is hutvā hoti, hutvā hoti." Encompassing both the name "hutvā hoti" of the future and the name of the present, it is challenged as "hutvā hoti, hutvā hoti." Similarly, the meaning is that it is challenged as "na hutvā na hoti, na hutvā na hoti."

"As if enveloped in darkness from all sides"—by this phrase, it is shown that one who is not enveloped in darkness should be able to admit it. Here, the distinction is that in the first method, the state of "hutvā hoti" again for a thing that has already been is challenged, while in the second method, the state of having the name "hutvā hoti" for each one in the future, etc., is challenged.

## 10. Explanation of the Discourse on Conventional Expression
In the Discourse on Conventional Expression (Vohārakathā), regarding the phrase "Or are the ear and so on [supramundane]?", there is no reason why, among objects (visaya) and subjects/possessors of objects (visayī) which are exclusively mundane, only the object should have a supramundane nature while the subjects do not. Just as the supramundane nature of the subjects is not established, so too the supramundane nature of the sound-base (saddāyatana), which is an object, is not established. Among those (objects and subjects), just as that sound-base, whose supramundane nature is not established, reaches a supramundane state (according to your view), so too the ear and so on reach a supramundane state. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: "Are those ear-faculties and so on also supramundane?"

The meaning "If it were to strike against the supramundane (ear), it would be a supramundane expression" should not be accepted. This is because, even if it is imagined that it strikes against the supramundane, the supramundane nature of the sound-base does not exist; thus, this meaning should not be taken. Although the author cites "by mundane knowledge" (lokiyena ñāṇena), the Pali text actually has "by consciousness" (viññāṇena). That consciousness is understood as ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa) because it is connected with the ear-sensitivity (sotapasāda). "Non-exclusivity" (anekantatā) means that the reason "it is mundane because it is known by mundane knowledge" would lead to non-exclusivity (indeterminacy) because it can occur in both the mundane and the supramundane.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Conventional Expression is finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Discourse on Cessation
"Does not desire two truths of suffering" means that the opponent does not desire those two truths of suffering which ought to have two types of cessation (namely, cessation not through deliberation and cessation through deliberation). By the Pali "not ceased through deliberation by supramundane knowledge" and so on, those formations (saṅkhāra) that cease without deliberation and do not occur are shown as "ceased without deliberation" (appaṭisaṅkhāniruddha). It does not mean the destruction after arising (momentary cessation). By showing it thus, it amounts to showing that cessation not through deliberation (appaṭisaṅkhā-nirodha) is the cessation consisting in non-occurrence (asamudācaraṇa-nirodha).

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Cessation is finished.

## 3. The Third Chapter
## 1. Explanation of the Discourse on Powers
The statement that the knowledge of the proficiency of the faculties (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) is unique (to the Buddha) means that although disciples (sāvaka) know the possible and the impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna) and so on in brief by way of summary, such as "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should regard any formation as permanent," they do not know the knowledge of the proficiency of the faculties even in brief, such as "He knows the disposition, he knows the underlying tendency." Therefore, it is called "unique" (asādhāraṇa).

The statement by the Elder Anuruddha, "I know the proficiency of the faculties of beings as it really is," was said with reference only to knowing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties such as faith (saddhā) and so on. It should be understood in this context that it does not refer to the Power of the Tathāgata (Tathāgatabala) which is the knowledge of the proficiency of the faculties mentioned above. It is said, "He claims [to know] by way of knowing the possible and impossible and so on in brief." If one claims thus, it would also mean claiming that "the Power of the Tathāgata is common to the disciples" in the same way. If that were so, how should this opponent be questioned?

The rejection regarding the remaining (knowledges) means that the proponent (Sakavādin) rejects them with reference to the part that is common, among the common and unique aspects of the knowledge of the possible and impossible and so on.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Powers is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Discourse on 'Noble'
For the person who makes a claim with reference to formations (saṅkhāra), it should be investigated how the meeting of two touches (phassa) occurs according to the method mentioned above. A being is called a "fixation" (paṇidhi) because of being established by being superimposed through false imagination. That fixation should not be established by superimposing it even on a single aggregate. Therefore, the state of being empty of that fixation (being) which is established by superimposing it even on a single aggregate is stated.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on 'Noble' is finished.

## 4. Vimuccamānakathā-vaṇṇanā
It should be examined what fault lies in this view: "The mind that has been liberated by liberation through suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti) due to jhāna is said to be 'being liberated' (vimuccamāna) by liberation through eradication (samuccheda-vimutti) at the moment of the Path (magga)." If there is a fault in pointing out the incomplete (vippakata), then in that description of the incomplete, that opponent says "liberated and being liberated" because it is in the process of being liberated. If there were a fault, one should not challenge the phrase "liberated and being liberated" (vimutta-vimuccamāna) as being liberated at the moment of arising (uppāda-khaṇa) of the Path and being liberated at the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-khaṇa); rather, one should only challenge the word "being liberated" (vimuccamāna). It is said to be an "abstract neuter" (bhāvana-napuṃsaka) because a part of the action of being liberated is a qualifier for the mind that is being liberated, either partially or in a part. "Kaṭādayo" means mats, clothes, and so on. "By a single mind" means by a single fruition consciousness (phala-citta).

## 7. Exposition of the Dibba-cakkhu-kathā
Upatthaddha (supported) means the infusion of power through the state (of the fourth jhāna) which is the cause for making it distinct through the power of repeated occurrence and the ability to take an object. Taṃ-mattam-eva means that the fleshly eye (maṃsa-cakkhu) as it was before, prior to the infusion of power, is not supported by the Dhamma. Anāpāthagata refers to things that have not come into the range of vision, which is the place to be grasped by the fleshly eye (i.e., things hidden by mountains, walls, etc.). Here, the intention is to show the similarity of the object and the dissimilarity of the power and range (ānu-bhāva-gocara). In taking the object as "What is the object of the fleshly eye?", it is not to show the distinction of the object, but rather to show such a visible object (rūpārammaṇa) in which there are special powers and ranges, or to show the distinction of the power and range even in the same object.

He does not wish that the fleshly eye itself is the divine eye means he does not wish that the fleshly eye as it was before is the divine eye at the time it is supported by the Dhamma. Saying "The arising of the fleshly eye is the path (magga)" is said only to show that the fleshly eye is a cause, and not to establish the state of being unclung-to (anupādinnatā) by that statement. Rūpāvacarikānaṃ means the great elements (mahābhūta) that have arisen due to the cause of fine-material sphere absorption (rūpāvacara-jhāna) are called "belonging to the fine-material sphere"; this is what that opponent intends. This same method applies to the word arūpāvacarikānaṃ. "He rejects it because there is no fine-material sphere mind at the moment of the formless sphere" means he rejects it because at that very moment, being of the fine-material sphere, it cannot be of the formless sphere.

Even if he does not wish for the divine eye supported by wisdom to be the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu), the meaning is that if someone, because of the support of the Dhamma, speaks of it as being a different kind of eye, then in his doctrine, there would be three eyes: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the eye of wisdom.

## Exposition of the Dibba-cakkhu-kathā is finished.

## 4. Commentary on Dānakathā

"To urge by the power of the gift-object (deyyadhamma)" means to urge with the thought: if only the mental factor (intention/cetanā) is the gift (dāna), then by the meaning "it is called dāna because it is given," wouldn't the nature of dāna belong only to the mental factor of intention?

It should be understood that the word "aniṭṭhaphalā" (undesirable result) and so on is said for the purpose of showing the nature of dāna in non-mental things (such as food, etc.), and not for the purpose of showing the manifestation of the giving of results. By the word "aniṭṭhaphalā" and so on, it is as if the giving of results by non-mental things is stated, but it is not stating the nature of dāna; this word was said for the purpose of preventing that giving of results. Having done so, immediately after that, it was said, "Non-mental things such as food do not give a resultant (vipāka) in the future." "For the purpose of always determining the state of desirable results (iṭṭhaphalā)" means that there is no undesirable result of dāna in any way like the gift-object, but it is for the purpose of determining that it is certainly only a desirable result.

"Itarena" means by the method "it is called dāna because it is given." "Na pana ekenatthena" means that to refute the Theravāda (Sakavādī) view that "only the gift-object is dāna," the sutta evidence such as "faith, shame" is suitable in the opponent's view (Paravādī); the sutta such as "here someone gives food" is also the same. To refute the opponent's view that "only the mental factor is dāna" and to establish the view that "the mental factor is dāna," the sutta such as "faith, shame" is suitable in the Theravāda view. The sutta such as "here someone gives food" is suitable for establishing that "the gift-object is dāna." It should be noted that "na pana ekenatthena" was said with reference to this difference between the purpose of refutation and the purpose of establishment. Among those two views, just as in the opponent's view, for the sake of sutta evidence, the meaning "only the mental factor" should be noted in the question "it should not be said that the mental factor is dāna," likewise, in the question "it should not be said that the gift-object is dāna," the meaning "only the gift-object" should be noted. In the context of "the gift-object has a desirable result," here, by the text "iṭṭhaphalābhāvamatāmeva paṭikkhittaṁ," only the absence of desirable results is refuted...

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion on "Is the Earth a Result of Kamma?" (Pathavī-kamma-vipāko-ti-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

By the statement that contact (phassa) is of various kinds such as that to be experienced as pleasant (sukha-vedanīya), etc., all results of kamma (kamma-vipāka) are shown through contact. Then, to show the association with states such as feeling (vedanā) and perception (saññā) which are excluded from itself (contact), it is said, "That contact and those perceptions, etc." The phrase "it exists for them" is said referring to the co-nascent states such as eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) together with advertence (āvajjana). Among those (results), whatever desired result there is, "longing for that result" means they perform kamma by longing only for the desired result; thus it shows the longing which is a decisive support (upanissaya) for kamma. Alternatively, craving (taṇhā) which has present feeling as its condition causes suffering to arise through the power of producing grasping (upādāna), etc. "Root craving" (mūla-taṇhā) refers either to the craving in a previous life which is the decisive support for the kamma that produces the present round of results (vipāka-vaṭṭa), or to the craving which is the companion of kamma and the decisive support for the result.

To show the suitability in the challenge even by the power of their own view, he said, "Also by the view of those," and so on.

By the words "by the power of obtaining," he shows that when there is kamma, there is the obtaining of the earth, etc.; thus kamma is said to be "conducive to that (result)."

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Intermediate State (Antarābhava) is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Discussion on the Strands of Sensual Pleasure (Kāmaguṇa)

The state of being sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) due to the sense of being desired should be understood with the intention that all sense-sphere aggregates etc. are called sense-sphere existence. However, the state of being sense-sphere existence only for the grasped aggregates (upādinnakkhandha) is shown in the Dhātukathā, but not the state of being sense-sphere existence due to the sense of being desired. Relying on the mere words "Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure," because only the five portions of sensual pleasure are called "sensual pleasure" (kāma), the term "sense element" (kāmadhātu) is not the name of anything else; this is the meaning of "relying on the mere words" with this intention.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Strands of Sensual Pleasure is finished.

515-516. 517-518. "The nose-signs also" (ghānanimittāni pi)—this statement should be understood as "the signs of the nose etc." "Sign" (nimitta) refers to the collection of matter having such a shape that is marked as the location for the nose-sensitivity (ghānapasāda) etc.

524-526. Subtle matter exists; the escape from that subtle matter is the immaterial state (āruppa); this is the meaning.

527-537. "Those who are planning/striving" (pakappayamānā) means those who are exerting effort, those who are performing excessive activity regarding the associated phenomena (sampayutta-dhamma). ## 10. Explanation of the Discussion on the Life Faculty (Jīvitindriya)

In the problem of "immaterial life faculty" (arūpa-jīvitindriya), the entire problem starting with "Do immaterial phenomena have life (āyu)?" is stated up to the final phrase. Where it is desired that "immaterial phenomena have a life-faculty continuity that is dissociated from mind (cittavippayutta)", the opponent (paravādī) who desires that life-faculty continuity dissociated from mind for both material and immaterial phenomena is justified in saying it for immaterial phenomena as well. Thus, it should be noted that "for immaterial phenomena" (arūpadhammānaṃ) is said.

By the Pali text starting with "Do material phenomena occur in the continuity of beings?", it should be understood that it refers to that same life-faculty continuity dissociated from mind.

"With reference to the preceding and succeeding parts" means that because of the proximity to the attainment (samāpatti), even at that time [of entering], one is indeed called an attainer (samāpanna) at that moment; this is the meaning.

544-545. In the phrase "two life faculties," the earlier reading is "the question of the proponent (sakavādī), the admission of the other (paravādī)". The later reading is "the question of the opponent (paravādī), the admission of the proponent (sakavādī)"; that later reading alone is appropriate.

By the Pali "the rest" (sesaṃ), it refers to the group of terms such as "stream-enterer" (sotāpanna) etc., which precede this inquiry: "the cause of action such as killing (pāṇātipātādi-kammassa hetu)." The phrase "Well then" (handa hi) is only the word of admission of the opponent, so it is not proper to say "to make [him] admit" (sampaṭicchāpetuṃ). In fact, it would be appropriate to say that the proponent (sakavādī) speaks in order to make that opponent admit, "What is the cause of which action?". Alternatively, in the word "to make admit" (sampaṭicchāpetuṃ), without taking the meaning "to make [him] admit the portion of the view," it should be understood that the opponent speaks in order to make the proponent accept his own view.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Cause of Action is finished.

## 9. Ninth Chapter (Navamavagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Discussion of One Who Sees the Benefits (Ānisaṃsadassāvīkathā)

'Vibhāgadassanatthaṃ' means for the purpose of showing the distinction.

It should be examined how the refutation of the opponent's view, who acknowledges [the point] by means of various states of mind, could be appropriate. It is appropriate to say that this Ānisaṃsakathā is undertaken for the purpose of showing the opponent, who asserts two types of seeing simultaneously by means of the object, that those two types of seeing cannot exist simultaneously.

By the words beginning with 'anussavavasena', it is shown that insight (vipassanā) is not only the knowledge having impermanence (anicca) etc. as its object, but also the knowledge that sees the benefit in Nibbāna, such as 'non-arising is security (khema)'.

'Suttabhayena' should be understood as being due to the fear of contradicting such a Sutta, because the Blessed One taught the state of security (khema) etc., referring to the state of being unyoked (asaṃyojaniya) etc., in the Sutta beginning with: 'Monks, that further shore is security, it is free from danger; this is a designation for Nibbāna'.

552-553. 554-556. It is said that they 'exist' only because they have not yet been abandoned by the Path; it does not mean they exist because they are manifest.

557-8. Regarding 'tassa ñāṇassa', they say it refers to the knowledge of the Path (maggañāṇa).

'Aviseseneva' means by both [ways], namely, by way of object and by way of association (sampayoga).

## 11. Commentary on the Discourse on Possession of Past and Future

568-570. "Tāsu" means in those designations (paññatti). One is called "samannāgata" (possessed of) because of the designation of possession (samannāgama-paññatti); one is called "lābhī" (possessor) because of the designation of attainment (paṭilābha-paññatti). ## 10. The Tenth Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Cessation

571-2. The commentator, in saying "simultaneously with the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) of the life-continuum mind (bhavanga-citta)" etc., also states that the resultant aggregates (vipāka-khandha) desired as the rebirth-process (upapatti-bhava) arise simultaneously with the moment of dissolution of the functional aggregates (kiriya-khandha). ## The Commentary on the Discourse on Cessation is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Path for One Endowed with the Fivefold Consciousness

"Taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ" (that characteristic) refers to the characteristic stated as "the fivefold consciousness has a base that has arisen" etc., without saying "the sixfold consciousness." Here, not saying "the sixfold consciousness" is intended to be the reason for the statement "Indeed, it should not be said..." etc.

"Lokiyo" refers to the mundane path of insight (vipassanā-magga). Therein, "yaṃ animittaṃ" (that which is signless) means that at the moment of being endowed with eye-consciousness, one who takes the signless is said to be not a taker of signs (nimitta); that very signless is the void (suññata).

584-586. "Inclines by way of wholesome or unwholesome" means it occurs by inclining through the nature of being wholesome or unwholesome. ## 6. Commentary on the Discourse on Two Virtues

587-589. This refers to cessation by way of momentary dissolution (khaṇabhaṅga), not cessation as non-occurrence, nor cessation as the transgression of virtue. "Like transgression" means that just as one becomes immoral when a transgression is committed, so too one is immoral even when it has ceased by momentary dissolution; this is the meaning of perceiving it as no different from transgression.

## 7. Commentary on the Discourse on Virtue being Non-mental

590-594. "Whereby that person is indeed called virtuous" means that because of the accumulation (upacaya) of kamma which is virtue, existing without being associated with the mind, even one who is endowed with unwholesome or indeterminate minds is indeed called virtuous. 598-600. In the Commentary on the Cause of Undertaking, the statement that it is similar to the previous discourse should be understood as being similar to a portion of the Discourse on Enjoyment (Paribhoga-kathā).

## The Commentary on the Discourse on the Cause of Undertaking is finished.

## 11. Commentary on the Discourse on Non-intimation and Immorality

603-604. In the phrase "the fulfillment of the factor in killing etc. by command," if a person who is commanded on one day to kill another living being performs the killing on a subsequent day, then at the time of that killing, that previous command becomes the factor (cause) even without vocal intimation (vaci-viññatti). Therefore, it means immorality without intimation (aviññatti-dussīlya).

## 11. The Eleventh Chapter

## 4. Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge

614-615. In the Commentary on Knowledge, regarding the phrase "as for the Mahāsaṅghikas," there may be other Mahāsaṅghikas here besides the Andhakas mentioned previously in the Discourse on Knowledge without Objects (Kathāvatthu 557 etc.). By the phrase "if ignorance is gone" etc., it shows that just as the departure of lust (rāga) is the cause for the designation of a person as "lust-free" (vītarāga), the departure of ignorance (aññāṇa) is the cause for the designation of a person as "knowledgeable" (ñāṇī). Indeed, one is not called "knowledgeable" because knowledge exists in him, but rather one is called "knowledgeable" because of being the opposite of one who is ignorant. In the phrase "because of the attainment of knowledge," it should be understood that because ignorance (aññāṇa) has departed through the attainment of knowledge, that person arrives at the state of being fit to be called "knowledgeable."

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Discourse on "This is Suffering"

618-620. In the phrase "the other, however, in his own doctrine (sakasamaye)," it means the opponent (paravādī) in his own doctrine.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on "This is Suffering" is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Discussion on the Power of Psychic Potency

621-624. The phrase "or by the power of the result of kamma" is spoken with reference only to hell. Indeed, in that hell, the divisions such as Abbuda and so on are shown by the power of the result of such kamma. The phrase "or by the counting of years" is spoken with reference to humans and devas such as those of the Cātumahārājika realm. For those humans and devas, kamma that is capable of yielding results even for an incalculable period (asaṅkhyeyya) is delimited by the number of years.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Power of Psychic Potency is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Discussion on Concentration

625-626. "In the sense of placing evenly (samādhānaṭṭhena)" means it is called concentration (samādhi) because of the meaning of placing equally. The meaning is: without taking it that there is a distinct mental factor called one-pointedness (ekaggatā). "By way of a pretext (chaleṇa)" means that because of the fact of having a single thought-moment, there is no distinction between the concentration associated with eye-consciousness and the concentration associated with a meditative absorption (jhāna) mind; thus, the intention is [to speak] by way of such mere commonality.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Concentration is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Discussion on the Stability of Phenomena

"And the state of being a proximity condition (anantarapaccayatañceva)" means that ignorance (avijjā) assists formations (saṅkhārā) by way of proximity condition. There is that which is the standing or the cause of standing of ignorance; because of that standing or cause of standing, that proximity force (anantara-satti) arises. The meaning is that the standing or cause of standing, which is called the state of being a proximity condition, arises along with that standing or cause of standing.

In this context, the taking of the proximity condition should be understood as having the purpose of showing a single proximity condition that is devoid of the state of being a mutuality condition (aññamaññapaccaya). By showing that one type of condition, all conditions similar to that proximity condition are shown.

"And the state of being a mutuality condition (aññamaññapaccayatañca)" means that ignorance is a condition for formations, and formations are also conditions for ignorance. In that case, because of the standing or cause of standing called the state of ignorance being a condition for formations, the standing or cause of standing called the state of formations being a condition for ignorance arises; and because of that standing or cause of standing of formations, the other standing or cause of standing of ignorance arises. This is the meaning.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Stability of Phenomena is finished.
97:
## 10. Explanation of the Discussion on Impermanence

"Produced like form, etc. (rūpādayo viya parinipphannā)" means they are produced (parinipphanna) because they arise and cease together with form and so on. "By way of investigating the classification of impermanence (aniccatāvibhāgānuyuñjanavasena)" means that just as the term "stick" is used for three sticks, the term "impermanence" (anicca) is used for the three characteristics; thus, it is said to be by the power of investigating the specific distinctions of that impermanence.

## 12. The Twelfth Chapter

## 1. Explanation of the Discussion on Restraint and Action

630-632. "Resultant door (vipākadvāra)" refers to the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta). "Kamma door (kammadvāra)" refers to wholesome and unwholesome minds.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Restraint and Action is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Discussion on Kamma

633-635. "Rejection with reference to the indeterminate (abyākataṃ sandhāya paṭikkhepo)" means it is said that the rejection is made by way of the characteristic of one's own doctrine (sakavāda). Thinking that if the indeterminate (abyākata) volition is shown in its true nature, then the volition that yields results (wholesome and unwholesome) is also already shown, it was said: "In order to show the volition that yields results and the volition that does not yield results in their true nature."

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Kamma is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Discussion on "Sound is a Resultant"

636-637. By the words "Whether mental phenomena born of kamma (kammasamuṭṭhānā arūpadhammā vā)," etc., it is shown that even in the case of physical phenomena such as the eye which are born of kamma, the term "resultant" (vipāka) is not used; how much less, then, could there be any reason to call sound "resultant," which is not even born of kamma?

## The Explanation of the Discussion on "Sound is a Resultant" is finished.
98:
## 4. Explanation of the Discussion on the Six Sense Bases

638-640. In the phrase "Therefore, it is a resultant," it means that the view of certain people is that "all six sense bases are resultants," without specifying any particular sense base.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Six Sense Bases is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Discussion on the Seven-times-at-most [Person]

641-645. "Fixed as a seven-times-at-most person (sattakkhattuparama-tāniyato)" means one who is certain in the state of being a seven-times-at-most person. "This distinction" refers to this specific difference. "Do you desire the fixed certainty of that person?" means: do you desire a fixed certainty in another state of being a seven-times-at-most person by way of the state of one not subject to downfall (avinipāta-dhammatā) and the attainment of the fruition (phala) immediately after one's own path?

"The absence of heinous kamma (ānantariya-kammābhāvaṃ)" means the absence of that heinous kamma by which a person would be called one incapable of penetrating the Dhamma; or it means that the seven-times-at-most stream-enterer (sotāpanna) is not one who possesses heinous kamma. Indeed, if it is asked whether that person will penetrate the Dhamma within the seven lives, some teachers say: "The seven-times-at-most person does not exceed the seventh life, but there is no prohibition against attaining the Dhamma within those seven lives."

Other teachers, however, say: "For a person whom the Blessed One has predicted by the power of His knowledge, there is no such thing as penetration of the Dhamma within the seven lives; nevertheless, because there is no fixed certainty of lives, he is called 'capable' (bhabba). For example, just as wholesome super-knowledge volitions (abhiññā-cetanā) are called 'phenomena of the nature of result' (vipākadhamma-dhammā) because they have the capacity to give results when the cause is present, even if they do not give results at times; likewise, the seven-times-at-most person exists because of the weakness of the faculties (indriya), not because of the existence of a fixed certainty of lives (bhava-niyāma), nor because of the Blessed One's prediction. Furthermore, since the weakness of faculties is not a phenomenon that causes the state of being incapable (abhabba) of attaining the Dhamma within the seven lives, that person cannot be called 'incapable' (abhabba). The state of being incapable is denied here because of the absence of phenomena that cause such incapacity, but it does not mean the state of being capable (bhabba) of penetrating the Dhamma within the seven lives. If the seven-times-at-most person were to penetrate the Dhamma within the seven lives, he would become a 'Kolankola' person." However, without making a specific distinction, it is appropriate to call him "capable (bhabba)" due to his capable nature. In the phrase "There is no phenomenon that fixes the lives," the words "having seen" are omitted, or it should be connected forward as "does not predict."

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Seven-times-at-most [Person] is finished.

## The Explanation of the Twelfth Chapter is finished.

## 13. Terasamavagga

## 1. Kappaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

654-657. In the Kappaṭṭhakathā, "below" refers to the Iddhibalakathā (referring to the intended meaning).

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Kappaṭṭhakathā.

## 3. Anantarāpayuttakathāvaṇṇanā

660-662. In the Anantarāpayuttakathā, because this person (the instigator) has instigated an immediate offense (ānantariya-kamma), they are called "anantarāpayutta". ## 4. Niyatassaniyāmakathāvaṇṇanā

663-664. In this passage, "The remaining states belonging to the three planes are called undetermined (aniyata)", the phrase "states belonging to the three planes" is said with reference to those states that have not yet reached the assurance (niyāma) [of rightness or wrongness]. Indeed, with reference to those very persons, it is said, "Even though endowed with those states, they are still undetermined." Thus, taking only this conventional usage, those who hold the view, "The destined Bodhisatta, who is in his final existence (pacchimabhavika), is capable of penetrating the Dhamma and entering [the assurance]," interpret the meaning as "He enters the assurance." In this way, the mere existence of the designation "destined" (niyata) is stated as the reason for the word "niyato", and the capability to penetrate the Dhamma is stated as the reason for the words "niyāmaṃ okkamati". However, it is more appropriate to say that the capability (bhabbatā) itself is the reason for both. The phrase "by another reason" means that if a destined person were to enter the assurance—if one destined for wrongness (micchattaniyata) were to enter the assurance of rightness (sammattaniyāma), or one destined for rightness were to enter the assurance of wrongness—it is stated to show that such a thing does not exist.

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Niyatassaniyāmakathā.

## 8. Asātarāgakathāvaṇṇanā
In the Asātarāgakathā, greed that arises in the form "Oh, may this very thing be mine!" (aho vata me etadeva bhaveyya) is intended here as "lust" (rāga), and it shows that it is not intended in any other way. The word "Sutte pana" is connected with the word "adhippāyo".

676-680. Because it is called "craving for states" (dhamma-taṇhā), taking the craving that arises for wholesome states or for all supramundane states as "craving for states", it shows the view that because that state is craving, it is not wholesome, and because it arises regarding states (Dhamma), it is not unwholesome, thus it is "indeterminate" (abyākata). ## 1. Kusalākusalapaṭisandahanakathāvaṇṇanā
686-690. The word "taṃ" should be seen as connected separately to "wholesome" and "unwholesome". Alternatively, it should be seen as an ellipsis for "taṃ ubhayaṃ" (both of them). "Paṭisandahati" means it connects, or it means it causes to arise immediately after.

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Kusalākusalapaṭisandahanakathā.

## 2. Saḷāyatanuppattikathāvaṇṇanā
691-692. Some theorists (such as the Kapila teachers) say, "In the sprout, the mere seed of trees and so on, which are endowed with branches, twigs, etc., becomes manifest." Desiring to show their view as an illustration, he said "sampannasākhāviṭapānaṃ", and so on.

693-697. In the passage, "Dependent on the eye and forms, ear-consciousness arises," when it is said that one admits this by the power of one's own view, even though one notices the arising of ear-consciousness immediately after eye-consciousness, that person does not intend ear-consciousness that takes a form as its object at the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda); rather, they intend only the taking of a sound as its object at the ear-sensitivity (sota-pasāda). 698-699. The opponent (paravādī), who desires that the path-factors such as right speech are both form (rūpa) and the path (magga), also says "noble form" (ariyarūpa).

In the Dhammakathā, regarding the Pali "rūpaṭṭhato aññassa rūpassa abhāvā": that which is called the nature of change (the essence of matter) is said to be the fixed nature (niyāma) of matter. There is no such thing as the nature of change of matter that is distinct from matter itself. Therefore, matter is not a nature other than the nature of change of matter. Thus, matter is only the nature of change; it does not have the nature of feeling (vedanā) and so on. With this intention, it should be said that "matter is fixed by the nature of matter" (rūpaṃ rūpaṭṭhena niyataṃ). It should not be said otherwise, meaning it is not fixed by a nature of matter that is distinct from the matter itself—this is the intention of the Commentator.

In that passage "rūpaṭṭhato aññassa rūpassa abhāvā" etc., when it is shown that there is no nature of change of matter distinct from matter, it is as good as showing that there is no matter distinct from the nature of change of matter. Therefore, desiring to show precisely the absence of a nature of change distinct from matter, he said "rūpasabhāvo hi" etc.

"Esa vohāro" means: the nature of matter is 'rūpasabhāva', the essence of matter is 'rūpaṭṭha'. These terms, 'rūpasabhāva' and 'rūpaṭṭha', which are used as if taking them to be distinct, are for the purpose of making known that such a nature is indeed different and distinct from feeling (vedanā) and so on.

"Tasmā" means: because matter is not distinct from the essence of matter (rūpaṭṭha). The statement of the Sakavādin (proponent), who says "matter is fixed by the nature of matter" instead of directly saying "matter is only matter, it does not have the nature of feeling etc.," is also faulty in the manner already stated. If it is faulty, why is it accepted? If it is asked thus: because the statement "matter is fixed by the nature of matter" should be said with the intention that "matter is only the nature of change, it does not have the nature of feeling etc."; therefore, when it is said, the meaning should be noted that he accepts the proposition "matter is fixed by the nature of matter."

If it is objected: "This statement 'matter is fixed by the nature of matter' is said by oneself (the Sakavādin) and not by another (the Paravādin); therefore, is it not improper to say he 'accepts' it?"—it is not so; it is proper to say so because one speaks of oneself as if speaking of another. Alternatively, in the word "vattabbaṃ," it means it should be said by the Sakavādin. If that Sakavādin should say it and if he accepts this meaning, then this is the very meaning already stated as to why the Sakavādin accepts it.

"Atthantaravasena" means: because the opponent (Paravādin) made an objection by concealing the proper reason already stated in the commentary—that "matter is only matter, it does not have the nature of feeling etc."—he (the Commentator) shows that very reason and prevents the objection. ## 23. Tevīsatima-vagga

## 1. Ekādhippāya-kathā-vaṇṇanā

By the intention of compassion, "one having a single intention" means having an intention other than the intention of lust. In this term "eko adhippāyo," the word "eka" should be understood in the sense of being the same (samāna). When the word "eka" is in the sense of "same," even in the intention of lust, there is the state of having a single intention as "ekādhippāyena."

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Having a Single Intention is finished.

## 3-7. Issariya-kāmakārikā-kathā-vaṇṇanā

910-914. Being able to act as one wishes through one's own mastery is called "issariya-kāmakārikā." "Gaccheyya" means one would go to the descent into the womb.
116:
In this passage, "issariya-kāmakārikā-hetu nāma dukkarakārikā micchādiṭṭhiyā karīyati," it should be understood that what is called difficult practice (dukkarakārikā), when performed because of the cause of being able to act according to one's will due to mastery over the mind, is performed with wrong view. Or, it should be understood that there is no such thing as "issariya-kāmakārikā-hetu" performed apart from wrong view.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Acting According to One's Will through Power is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Discussion of Counterfeits

915-916. Referring to states such as loving-kindness (mettā), in the problem "Is there any state that is not lust but has a nature similar to lust (a counterfeit of lust), like loving-kindness etc.?", it takes lust itself; the same applies to hatred (dosa).

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Counterfeits is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Unperfected

917-918. In the passage "na aniccādibhāvaṃ," because this matter (rūpa) has an inherent nature such as impermanence, that matter is called "aniccādibhāva." The commentator, by saying "na kevalañhi paṭhamasaccameva dukkhaṃ," shows that the question "dukkhaññeva parinipphannaṃ" is asked with reference to the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). This being so, that proponent (Sakavādin) should not say "cakkhāyatanaṃ aparinipphannaṃ" etc. Because states such as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) are neither non-grasped (anupādinna) states nor supramundane (lokuttara) states that are not included in the truth of suffering. "Taṃ" means "only suffering is perfected (parinipphanna), but matter is not"; because matter is also suffering, the meaning is "O friend, it should not be said."

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Unperfected is finished.
